Hybrid Modeling for Bioprocesses: Architectures,
Applications, and Perspectives
Grupo de Investigación en Aplicación de Nuevas Tecnologías (GIANT) Departamento de Ingeniería Química, Universidad Nacional de Colombia Sede
Manizales, Campus La Nubia, Manizales, Colombia
Recent hardware developments within industrial digitalization make more evident the need of high-fidelity models to exploit
process system engineering potential in biomanufacturing. Hybrid models, which combine first-principles (white-box) and
data-driven (black-box) approaches, aim to leverage the strengths of both methodologies to mitigate their individual limitations
to provide high predictive power. This article explores the integration of hybrid modeling techniques in bioprocess engineering, emphasizing their potential to facilitate product development, accelerate experimental design, enhance process monitoring,
drive optimization and catalyze the implementation of digitalization strategies to achieve a more robust and sustainable production in the framework of the goals set by the UN 2030 agenda. In this review, we analyze 270 publications from the early
1990s to 2024, extracting application domains, hybrid-model architectures, implementation software, and nonparametric output
structures. Our findings highlight marked improvements in predictive accuracy, and extrapolation capabilities while revealing
persistent challenges in integrating mechanistic and empirical components. This review on hybrid modeling implementations
shows their potential to enhance accuracy, calibration, and extrapolation capabilities, highly required for bioprocesses. This work
underscores the importance of integrating mechanistic and data-driven approaches to improve the flexibility and interpretability
of models in complex engineering systems, offering significant implications for more sustainable and innovative bioprocesses.

Introduction
Sustainability has become a critical focus in addressing global
challenges, as it ensures that current development meets the
needs of present generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), set by the United Nations,
provide a comprehensive framework to tackle pressing issues
such as climate change and environmental degradation. Among
these, goals like Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG9),
Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12), Climate
Action (SDG 13), and Life Below Water (SDG 14) are directly
impacted by how industries operate, making sustainable practices essential [1].
As of 2024, the SDGs were in a dire situation, with most of them
being severely delayed and targets not on track to being met [1].
For SDG 9, less than 20% of the targets were on track to being
met, whereas for SDG 12 the share was around 30%. Moreover,
the UN estimates that 84% of the SDG targets have either stagnated or shown a reversal of progress. This indicates that further
acceleration is needed to achieve the targets. Research in diverse

areas of knowledge and articulation with industry is crucial to
meet the 2030 agenda [1].
In the framework of the above-mentioned goals, biorefineries
emerge as an attractive approach to achieve them. Second and
third generation biorefineries (2G and 3G) allow biomass and
agricultural wastes to take full potential, without compromising
food security, which in turn makes them very attractive for adding
value to waste [2]. Bioprocesses offer a promising avenue to meet
sustainability goals by reducing reliance on fossil fuels and lowering carbon footprints [3]. However, they also pose significant
challenges, including the complexity of biological systems and
the need to balance economic viability with ecological responsibility [4]. Moreover, biorefineries are often complex processes
that involve many steps, posing a technical challenge from their
inception through the implementation.
One of the main challenges of biorefineries takes place in the
bioreaction stage. Biotransformations are intricate, and their
mechanisms are usually not well understood, which leads to low
titer, productivity, and yield.
Process systems engineering (PSE) plays a vital role in addressing these challenges by integrating knowledge from engineering,
mathematics, and computer science to optimize bioprocesses [5].
PSE methods enable the design, control, and operation of bioprocess systems in a way that improves efficiency and minimizes
environmental impact. For instance, through advanced modeling, simulation, and optimization techniques, PSE can help predict the behavior of biological systems, optimize resource usage,
and identify bottlenecks in production [6, 7].
In PSE, modeling takes a central role for process simulation and
its use [8, 9]. Models can administrate information from two main
perspectives: structural (our understanding of the underlying
mechanisms) and the model parametrization (the nature of the
numeric techniques used to describe the relationships between
data). From the structural point of view, first-principles, mechanistic or phenomenological models represent a wide class of models, usually called white-box, due to being developed primarily on
conservation equations and physical laws. First principles models
are constructed through deductive reasoning, wherein the model
equations are derived from existing knowledge of the system,
using established relationships such as conservation laws. Mechanistic models usually comprise a system of differential algebraic
equations (DAEs). An important characteristic of mechanistic
models is that they can be extrapolated to process conditions outside of the calibration space, thanks in part to being developed
from conservation laws, although this is not always the case [10].
In contrast, data-driven models typically employ an inductive
approach, wherein a generic mathematical model is fitted to map
inputs to outputs, without considering the intrinsic structure of
the phenomena, unlike their white-box counterparts [10–12].
Data-driven techniques usually take the form of arbitrary functions to model the relations between inputs and outputs. Gray
models usually fall in between, combining mechanistic knowledge and data-driven techniques [13, 14].
From another perspective, models can be classified regarding
the form of model parametrization. Parametric models are established beforehand based on the knowledge of the process [15].

These models possess a finite number of parameters, often characterized by physical significance, which vary according to the
model’s complexity [11]. In contrast, nonparametric models are
solely derived from data, lacking predefined parameters [15]. The
term “nonparametric” does not mean that the model is built without parameters, but that the number of them is variable, not
fixed in advance by knowledge, and that they commonly lack
physical significance [11]. In nonparametric modeling, mathematical techniques such as algebraic, series expansions, machine
learning (ML), and other black-box approaches are used to derive
insights from inputs to outputs. These techniques are also called
“surrogate models” when they are used to approximate the behavior of more complex and computationally costly models [16] and
are used to describe the relevant process behavior exclusively
from model-generated data, to perform calculations faster such as
optimization [17, 18]. Typically, they have great predicting power
inside the space of their calibration, but extrapolation is not advisable [19].

not fully capture the system dynamics. Developing parametric
models requires extensive domain expertise, making the process
time-intensive and complex, often involving experts from multiple disciplines.
Nonparametric models offer greater flexibility as they do not
require prior mechanistic knowledge, making them particularly
useful when the underlying system is poorly understood or difficult to describe mathematically. These models can efficiently capture complex, nonlinear relationships within data, often uncovering hidden patterns that parametric models might miss. However,
their flexibility comes at a cost. Nonparametric models typically
require large amounts of high-quality data for training, and their
computational cost is significantly higher, particularly during the
training phase. Additionally, they are prone to overfitting and
overparameterization, making them less robust, and they often
struggle with extrapolation beyond the observed data range. They
are usually not reliable enough to extrapolate to conditions outside of their calibration space; however, they have great interpolation capabilities within it. Another critical drawback is their lack
of interpretability, as they do not rely on physical constraints or
conservation laws, which can make it difficult to understand the
underlying mechanisms driving predictions.
From previous experience, there is no ideal model, with both
parametric and nonparametric models having strengths and
shortcomings that not only depend on system understanding, but
also on data and computational power. As a potential trade-off,
the scientific community has proposed hybrid modeling, also
called hybrid semi-parametric modeling, to overcome the challenges that arise from parametric and nonparametric modeling,
while retaining most of their advantages.
Notice that researchers do not always agree on the definition
and use of the term “hybrid model.” Some authors claim to have
developed hybrid models, when they combine different mechanistic and empiric knowledge (mathematical relationships that
provide reliable approximations but are not built using mechanistic knowledge) such as correlations for heat and mass transfer
coefficients, for example, [28–34]. Besides, the term has been
used when modified structures apply to pure nonparametric
approaches for predictions. These modifications usually entail
combinations of artificial neural networks (ANNs) with other ML
techniques or optimization algorithms [35–40]. Finally, “hybrid
modeling” has been applied to other approaches such as Computational Fluid Dynamics applications that integrate various
numerical methods [41] and process system engineering simulations that use multiple software tools to perform the simulations [42–44]. Here in, “hybrid modeling” represents a modeling
paradigm that seeks to combine the strengths of both parametric
and nonparametric modeling while minimizing their individual
disadvantages.
Hybrid modeling is an emerging approach gaining traction; thus
there are recent reviews in the literature detailing the applications
of hybrid modeling to separation processes [45], biochemical processes using neural networks [24, 46, 47], wastewater treatment
(WTT) [48]; chemical, petroleum and energy systems [46, 49].
For bioprocesses specifically, recent reviews include topics such
as the role of hybrid models in bioprocess scale-up [50]; the applications of hybrid modeling to systems biology for mammalian

Literature Review Methodology
A comprehensive bibliometric study was performed to quantitatively and qualitatively map the research landscape using descriptors such as journals, publication outputs, institutions, authors,
and keywords. Full details of the methodology for the literature review can be found elsewhere [52]. Here, a summary is
presented.
The search strategy began with identifying the need for information, focusing on hybrid modeling applications in bioprocesses.
Non-biotechnological processes were excluded to maintain the
relevance of the field. Scopus and Web of Science were selected as
the primary databases due to their extensive and complementary
coverage of scientific literature. A search equation was designed
by expanding terms, incorporating keywords related to hybrid
models (e.g., “hybrid model,” “hybrid neural network”) and bioprocesses (e.g., “bio*,” “bioproc*”). The search was restricted to
publications from 1992, marking a seminal work in the field,
through March 2024. The search was repeated on December 2024
to encompass new publications.
Search results were refined by targeting specific fields: “TitleAbstract-Keywords” for Scopus and “Topics” for Web of Science. Abstracts were validated manually to ensure relevance
to Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, excluding unrelated
documents. This iterative process included refining the search
equation multiple times, guided by insights gained during analysis. The search continued until results stabilized, with less
than 5% variation in top authors, journals, and total results
across iterations. A total of 5890 contributions were found, and
after a manual review, 270 contributions were selected as of

Hybrid Modeling Framework
This section is divided into subsections to provide a clear and
comprehensive look at hybrid modeling. Section 3.1 introduces
the general characteristics of hybrid models, laying the groundwork for understanding their key features. Section 3.2 dives into
the different structures commonly used to implement these models, whereas Section 3.3 explores various ways to incorporate
knowledge into their design. Section 3.4 highlights some of the
most popular nonparametric substructures used in hybrid modeling for bioprocesses. Section 3.5 focuses on how the performance
of these models has been assessed, followed by Section 3.6, which
discusses the data requirements necessary for building them, and
lastly, Section 3.7 showcases some of the main applications of
hybrid models.
3.1
|
Main Characteristics of Hybrid Modeling
In the middle of the parametric and nonparametric modeling paradigms, the called “hybrid models” or “hybrid semiparametric models” exist, combining both first principles and
data-driven techniques to describe the systems. Figure 1 shows
the knowledge basis and mathematical representations for parametric, nonparametric, and hybrid modeling. Parametric models heavily rely on first principles and prior knowledge, using
conservation laws, mass-energy-momentum balances, kinetic
mechanisms, thermodynamic relationships, and transport laws

as algebraic equations, DAEs or partial differential equations
(PDEs), with data being mostly used for parameter identification
(hence the dotted green line in Figure 1). Nonparametric modeling approaches are usually data-hungry [23, 26, 45, 50] and
build their knowledge exclusively from process data, extracting
no information from first principles. Nonparametric models are
usually expressed as data-driven techniques such as ANNs, Gaussian Processes (GPs), and support vector machines (SVMs) or
Autoregressive models (ARX, ARMAX, ARIMA). Hybrid modeling aims to compromise both approaches in the middle, needing
fewer data than nonparametric models, but without requiring
prior knowledge as extensive as parametric models do. Hybrid
models can be expressed in a wide range of structures, mixing
the data-driven techniques used for nonparametric modeling and
the mechanistic knowledge expressed in parametric models. It
is important to note that hybrid models do not necessarily use
their parametric and nonparametric components in the same
ratio. Thus, the spectrum seen in Figure 1 signals that hybrid
models can be “darker” if they rely more on the nonparametric
techniques than the mechanistic ones, or “lighter” if the inverse
is true.
Literature often claims that hybrid modeling leverages most of
the advantages of parametric and nonparametric modeling while
minimizing its disadvantages. Although this is empirically seen
in an increased performance when compared against full mechanistic models, there are sparse mathematical proofs. It has been
proven that giving more structure to the nonparametric subcomponent via an additive term helps to reduce the asymptotic
variance of the parametric parameters [53]. Authors prove that
if the parametric model is ill conditioned, hybrid models will
outperform it. Furthermore, a Focused Information Criterion is

Hybrid modeling main characteristics are [25, 26, 49, 55]:
1. Hybrid models usually present better parameter estimation,
due to:
a. Less parameters than pure nonparametric techniques,
which can lead to higher statistical confidence of the
identified parameters.
b. The chance to map all measurable quantities as inputs to
the model structure, where the relationships are established using the nonparametric sub model. Thus, more
information is included than in parametric models, usually allowed due to deficiencies in process understanding.
c. Combining data-driven approaches with mechanistic
knowledge results in a constrained space that imposes
physical meaning and bounds to the variables, which is
hard to achieve in pure non-parametrical techniques.
d. When compared to pure nonparametric models, hybrid
modeling exhibits superior calibration properties and
enhanced extrapolation properties when compared to
pure nonparametric techniques due to the structuring of
the operation space using mechanistic or phenomenological knowledge. This structuring reduces the search
space, consequently requiring less data for training
hybrid models than for pure nonparametric approaches.
However, the strategies for training and validation of
hybrid models are heavily dependent on the model structure/architecture chosen.
2. Less mechanistic or first principles knowledge is needed for
developing a hybrid model than a complex pure parametric
model.
3. Hybrid models are usually developed faster than pure
parametric models, since less mechanistic knowledge is

3.2
|
Hybrid Model Design Patterns
Recently, a comprehensive overview of design patterns for hybrid
models was presented [26]. These design patterns generalize,
unify, and formalize diverse modeling approaches across various domains and applications. The following sections introduce
these patterns and illustrate them through selected relevant studies from the literature. Notice that the chemical engineering literature has used the term “architecture” [11, 23, 56]. Recently, a
distinction between “design pattern” and “architecture” was proposed because any model architecture can have different combinations of different design patterns, working in parallel, in series
or nested inside another [26]. In the present work, “architecture”
and “design pattern” are synonyms, whereas “structure” is used
to discuss the different combinations and arrangements of the
design patterns. It is important to note that a model structure can
comprise one or several design patterns.
Agarwal [56] presented the general architectures in which the
white box and black box components of a hybrid model can be
arranged. Figure 2 shows three configurations. Configurations
(a) and (b) show a serial architecture, where a black box output serves as input for the white box, and the white box output
serves as input for the black box, respectively. Configuration (c)
shows a parallel architecture, and finally, configuration (d) shows
a data-driven technique constrained by a parametric model. Configurations (a), (b), (c), and (d) are also called “feature learning,”
“physics-based preprocessing,” “delta model,” and “physical constraints,” respectively [26]. In Figure 2 there are two types of
inputs for configurations (a), (b), and (c), named x1 and x2 (color
coded blue and green, respectively) to clarify that the inputs for
the different subcomponents of hybrid models might be different,
but also could include common variables.

The design pattern choice not only influences the interaction
between the different components of a hybrid model, but also
determines the training strategy and, therefore, computational
cost of developing a model.
3.2.1
|
Serial Architectures
The most popular hybrid model architecture is the “feature learning” design pattern. In this architecture, the white box is usually
composed of conservation laws, mass, heat, or momentum transfer relations that describe the process. The black box typically
represents the kinetics of the process or the transport coefficients,
for which there is no general valid model [10, 47, 57]. This architecture is very useful when there is no precise knowledge of the
underlying mechanisms, but there is enough data to identify the
underlying patterns. Another scenario is presented when there is
a huge amount of data that can be exploited to model the underlying mechanisms [58, 59].
The “physics-based preprocessing” design pattern is mostly used
in data sparse environments, primarily using data augmentation
[12]. In this architecture, the white-box model predictions are
used to establish a link between the state of the system and certain parameters [11]. Some examples include: the prediction of
cell culture using ANNs [60] where authors used an ANN to
model some reaction rates in their dynamic balance flux model
using other mechanistic reaction rates and states and inputs to
the data-driven components, a fed-batch process for producing
penicillin [61] taking advantage of Kalman filters to estimate
and reconstruct some states from noisy data and predict fault
detections, the control of biomass in protein production using
Pichia pastoris [62] implementing a soft-sensor to predict biomass
concentration based on online measurements of CO2 utilizing a
multi-linear regression that takes advantage of the mechanistic
carbon balance.
When utilizing serial architectures, the training can be done in
two different ways: coupling the identification of the parametric
and nonparametric components simultaneously or decoupling
the identification, usually calibrating a parametric structure and
then calibrating a nonparametric component to account for the
deficiencies of the parametric component.
3.2.2
|
Parallel Architecture
The parallel architecture (“delta model” design pattern) applies
if there is a process model (white box) that captures the underlying mechanisms but has limited predictive power due to structural factors not accounted for (unmodeled effects, nonlinearities, dynamic behavior) [26]. The predictive power of the model
can be enhanced using nonparametric techniques, although their
performance remains poor outside of the training region [11, 23].
This structure is interesting if the system can be decoupled into
non-interacting parts, that is, static non-linear and dynamic linear behavior. This modeling approach has been applied to cases
such as predicting phosphorus removal in a WTT process [63] correcting the model’s mismatch by adding the output of an ANN
to the mechanistic reaction rates to enhance prediction capabilities; using Kalman filters to correct bias from mechanistic model

Researchers have proposed three main ways for approaching the

or subtracted from the white box model prediction to enhance

used parallel structure, first proposed in bioprocesses to study a

“multiplication” because the output of the model is the multiplication of the outputs predicted by the black box and white
box, working as a correction factor (amplification or mitigation
of the parametric outputs). It was first utilized in bioprocesses
for a bakers’ yeast production process [17]. The (c) configuration
is applied when the outputs of the black box and white box are
transformed by either a black box or a white box model [69], as
such, weight factors (w1 and w2) are applied to combine them and
obtain the final prediction. It is important to note that the inputs
to the nonparametric and parametric parts could be different (as
evidenced in Figure 3); therefore, the nonparametric component
might obtain knowledge from information that the parametric
models do not consider in their formulation.
3.2.3
|
Physical Constraints
Physical constraints represent a hybrid modeling design pattern that integrates domain knowledge—such as conservation
laws—into the structure, parameters, or outputs of a data-driven
model [20, 26, 70]. These constraints can be categorized as hard
constraints and soft constraints, based on how strictly they are
enforced.
• Hard constraints encode physical principles directly into
the model’s structure, ensuring they are never violated.
For instance, adding a ReLU (rectified linear unit function,
which is a function that is 0 when its input is less than or
equal to 0 and is a linear function when its input is greater
than 0) activation layer to guarantee non-negative outputs
for variables like concentrations or pressure, or using a softmax layer to ensure molar fractions sum to one, are common examples [71]; or using Neural ODEs to predict ethanol
production via fermentation [72] or Chinese Hamster Ovary
cells (CHO) biomass growth in a bioreactor [73]. However,
hard constraints require the input data to align with the

imposed rules, a process known as data reconciliation [20].
A challenge with hard constraints is that they can result in
non-differentiable models complicating gradient-based optimization methods [26].
• Soft constraints incorporate mechanistic insights into the
loss function as penalties. These penalties guide the model
during training to produce outputs that align with domain
knowledge, allowing some flexibility in how strictly the constraints are followed [20, 26]. Once training is complete, the
model relies solely on the data-driven architecture, with the
domain knowledge encoded implicitly. Physics-informed
neural networks (PINNs) are an example of soft-constrained
models [70]. PINNs have been successfully applied to simulated cases of bioprocesses [74, 75]; kinetics of biodiesel
production [76]; and WTT plants [75].
When using hard constraints at the output, the results are guaranteed to be physically plausible; however, these constraints
can introduce non-differentiable nonlinearities that complicate
gradient-based optimization. To address this, soft constraints are
sometimes used because they provide a smoother optimization
landscape, even though they do not guarantee exact adherence
to the desired conditions. Moreover, combining multiple physical constraints in a single model can be challenging. A key benefit
of incorporating physical constraints is enhanced data efficiency.
By embedding prior knowledge into the model, the complexity of
the problem can be reduced, which in turn lowers the amount of
training data needed [26].

Knowledge Integration
The standard way to incorporate mechanistic knowledge into a
hybrid model is using mathematical expressions such as conservation laws or underlying phenomena. But they are not the only
form of knowledge that can be incorporated. Some examples are:
• Knowledge about different stages of a process (e.g., growth
phase; lag phase; etc. for a fermentation) can be leveraged
to apply fuzzy logic (FL) either to enhance prediction for
each phase by changing the mechanistic model [77–80] or
to change the structure of ANNs [81].
• Design of experiments can evaluate and optimize the black
box structure [82].
• Constraints can be added to the output predictions of the
hybrid model to enhance its performance [25].
• Physics laws can be encoded in the training phase of the
black-box component as in Physics Informed Neural Networks [47].
Mechanistic knowledge should be incorporated only if it is highly
certain, which means that it does not contain empirical assumptions to avoid producing a model with high bias. The white box
should be limited to knowledge that represents the physical interactions of the system [25]. For example, mass balances can be
incorporated without hesitation, as the mass conservation laws
apply to all systems. Assumptions like lumped parameters in a

therefore, the assumption introduces bias to the model.
The unknown elements of a hybrid model, such as kinetic terms,
unknown or unmeasured variables, or mass transfer coefficients
are usually represented by a nonparametric structure.
3.4
|
Data Driven Components of Hybrid
Models
Since the beginning of the century, the increasing availability of
data, driven by the continuous advancement of better and more
precise sensors, larger databases, and enhanced computational
power, has compelled engineers to recognize data as a valuable
source of information [12]. Therefore, mathematical techniques
that build insights from data are highly valuable. Non-parametric
and data-driven techniques can be broadly classified in the following categories, with accompanying examples of their applications to bioprocesses:
• Algebraic expressions such as polynomials or rational functions for predicting the pH and acetic acid production of
Kombucha fermentations [83], and sigmoidal and exponential functions for describing methane production during the
anaerobic digestion of orange peel waste [84].
• Series expressions such as Fourier series used for optimizing
the pH profile for controlling the process of the yeast Wickerhamomyces anomalus against the spoilage yeast Zygosaccharomyces rouxii in wine pre-fermentation [85].
• Statistical models such as principal component analysis
(PCA) for identifying the correlations between variables for
monoclonal antibodies production [86], and multivariate
data analysis (MVDA) for predicting the production of adenovirus using human embryonic kidney cells (HEK 293) [87].
• Time-series autoregressive approaches such as ARMAX for
controlling dissolved oxygen in a S. cerevisiae fermentation [88], ARIMA for modeling and predicting a membrane
bioreactor (MBR) for treating ampicillin from pharmaceutical wastewater [89] or ARX for predicting biomass concentrations in a lactic acid fermentation [90].
• ML approaches such as ANNs, as well as techniques like
GPs or SVMs [91]. An overview of several nonparametric
structures such as ANNs, Random Forests (RF), SVMs, GPs,
among others has been recently presented [92].
The choice of nonparametric technique coupled with the hybrid
model’s structure heavily influences the development and the
strategy for training and validation of the model.
3.5
|
Hybrid Model Performance Assessment
Hybrid models’ performance and extrapolation capabilities are
directly related to the structure of the nonparametric portion of
the model. This refers not only to whether the architecture is parallel or serial but also to the configuration and the specific model
structure of the nonparametric model, particularly its size (e.g.,

layers of an ANN, number of neurons per layer, type of activation
function, etc.) [11].
The size of the data-driven technique can be assessed using the
Akaike Information Criteria (AIC) or Bayesian Information Criteria (BIC), the latter being preferred for models with a high number of parameters [55, 57]. For discriminating between models,
Friedman’s test can be applied [93]. In general, there should be a
trade-off between estimation quality and the number of parameters, to avoid overfitting or underfitting issues, which should also
be addressed in training and validation.
To compare hybrid models’ performance to traditional parametric and nonparametric models, researchers have also used
more conventional metrics such as the coefficient of determination r2 despite not being suited for nonlinear estimators in biochemical systems [94], the mean squared error (MSE) and its
derivatives such as root mean square error (RMSE) or normalized MSE (NMSE), error measurements such as mean absolute
percentage error (MAPE), mean absolute error (MAE), among
others.
When extrapolating the hybrid model’s predictions outside the
training domain, some assessment of the validity of the extrapolation should be done. Authors have mainly used two complementary criteria: convex-hull criteria and a confidence interval criterion. The convex-hull criteria are used to verify that
each empirical model solely interpolates the data gathered during model identification. Meanwhile, the confidence interval
criterion evaluates the confidence intervals for the predictions
of the hybrid model [95]. Other authors have proposed that the
confidence interval of the hybrid model can be estimated using
Bayesian optimization, resampling the model’s prediction using
Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations [96].
3.6
|
Hybrid Modeling Requirements for Data
Data is essential for discerning the structure and parameters of
the hybrid model, and principally all properties of the model
(such as prediction quality and extrapolation capabilities) heavily rely both on the quality and quantity of the data [10, 12,
24]. Data is necessary to develop any hybrid model. If there is
no previous data, it must be generated, with a systematic exploration of the design space (e.g., using Design of Experiments
for a system or a benchmark model). Different techniques can
be applied, such as factorial design, sequential design, optimal
design, and model-based design methodologies [97]. A valuable alternative is the so-called “Intensified Design of Experiments,” where intra-experimental shifts to key parameters are
performed to capture the dynamics of the process [59, 98, 99].
This methodology has been applied specifically to develop hybrid
models, yielding great predictive power with a reduced number
of experiments in an early stage of model development. Intensified design of experiments has been paired with hybrid models
to transfer knowledge from lab scale to pilot scale in CHO cultures [100], reducing the number of experiments by as much as
50% while retaining the same levels of accuracy in monoclonal
CHO line producing immunoglobulin G4 monoclonal antibody
[101, 102], describing the design space with similar accuracy as a
full-factorial design of experiments despite having less than 33%

Hybrid Modeling Implementation
Recently, a comprehensive bibliometric analysis [52] spanning
360 contributions revealed that the hybrid modeling of bioprocesses is a growing research area, with an annual growth rate
of 9% since its inception in 1992. Recent advancements, particularly post-2017, underscore the impact of heightened awareness surrounding artificial intelligence and the integration of
next-generation ML techniques into hybrid models. Key themes
driving this field include “hybrid model,” “neural networks,”
and applications ranging from fermentation to biopharmaceutical manufacturing. A keyword network analysis identified three
central research clusters: process control applications, computational techniques, and the broader integration of bioprocessing
terminology with ML concepts.
This review builds on these findings, delving into quantifying
trends, innovations, and challenges in hybrid modeling for bioprocesses, setting the stage for a comprehensive examination of
the current state of the field to identify trends such as the types of
hybrid modeling on bioprocesses, the preferred design patterns,
the most used nonparametric techniques, the scale of the experimental data for developing the models, the mode of operation of
the experiments, software used for building the models, as well as

Synthesis of Key Findings
Hybrid models in bioprocesses predominantly employ ANNs as
the data-driven component, accounting for 58% of publications.
ANNs have been widely applied across various bioprocesses, from
cell cultivation to pharmaceutical production. Other ML techniques, such as SVMs, have also been utilized, particularly in
cell cultivation and WTT. In lesser proportion, parametric techniques such as polynomials and sigmoidal expressions have been
applied successfully to metabolic fluxes analysis [136], and lutein
production [139]. From an application perspective, various categories of data-driven techniques have been successfully employed
in bioprocessing. However, there is no consensus on the most
suitable method for each process type, despite a clear preference
for ANNs.
Over 63% of work targets metabolite production—chiefly fermentation and protein synthesis—while ̃40% address pharmaceutical operations (penicillin, therapeutic proteins, antibodies,
CHO cells) [101, 102]. As such, the enhanced prediction capabilities of hybrid models combined with specific approaches
to experimental design [59, 98, 99] have led to innovation in
the field. WTT comprises ̃10% of cases but leads in industrial
uptake, underscoring hybrid models’ aptitude for revealing hidden dynamics under sparse monitoring.
In terms of hybrid model architecture, feature learning hybrids
dominate despite offering no statistically significant performance
advantage over delta or serial patterns. Their popularity likely
stems from built-in interpretability, conservation law enforcement, and modular training, which suit the multi-step, partially
observed nature of bioprocesses [20].
Ethanol fermentations of S. cerevisiae remain the most intensely
studied system—driven by abundant data—while recent work
has diversified to include E. coli, P. pastoris, CHO cells (collectively 30%), and a broad “other” category (32%). Studies equally
showcase hybrid models across batch (44.6%), fed batch (33.7%)
and continuous (20.7%) modes of operation and at lab (53%),
pilot (25%) and industrial (21.7%) scales, underscoring their
adaptability [119].

19 of 30
Software choice and model evaluation are areas of persistent inconsistency. MATLAB remains the predominant simulation environment, although Python is gaining traction.
Model performance assessment still is variant: about a quarter of studies still rely on r2—despite its failure to penalize
over parameterization and insensitivity to nonlinear dynamics [94, 254]. On the other hand, 45% of contributions use
MSE derivatives to calculate their performance indexes, despite
it being highly sensitive to outliers [255]. This last selection
might be since it is a default performance index in ML toolboxes. To foster more robust and interpretable assessments,
we foresee that these performance indexes could be complemented with information-theoretic and distribution-based measures (e.g., entropy coefficients, Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, Log-Cosh and quantile losses) and adopting principled
model-comparison criteria such as Watanabe Akaike Information Criterion (WAIC) or Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation Information Criterion (LOO-CVI) [256–259].
Despite three decades of development, hybrid bioprocess modeling still lacks standardized protocols for selecting design patterns, balancing mechanistic and data-driven components, quantifying uncertainty and defining data preprocessing workflows.
The field’s reliance on trial and error and experience—evidenced
by 374 individual model implementations versus 155 distinct
case studies—underscores this gap. Some efforts have been
made recently to highlight practical and technical details of
implementing hybrid models, such as reviews that present brief
guides for developing them [25, 260], but more work is needed.
Due to having both a parametric/mechanistic component and
a data-driven/nonparametric component, assessing how much
uncertainty comes from each remains an unexplored avenue. The
field could benefit from recent developments in the ML field,
where authors suggest a Monte Carlo approach to generate testing datasets and better capture uncertainty [261].
The absence of standardized guidelines in hybrid bioprocess
modeling arises precisely from its defining strength: structural flexibility. Hybrid frameworks can accommodate a wide
range of design choices—yet still outperform purely mechanistic
models—while demanding far less data than fully nonparametric approaches and preserving a degree of interpretability that
renders them practical for industrial deployment. However, this
very hybrid character also complicates evaluation: conventional
metrics and workflows developed for parametric or nonparametric models often fail to capture the unique tradeoffs in uncertainty
quantification and mechanistic parameter estimation inherent to
hybrid systems.
Numerical workflows in hybrid bioprocess modeling are similarly under specified. Critical steps—data pretreatment methods (both numerical and knowledge based), augmentation strategies, and the rationale for selecting inputs to the data driven
module—are frequently omitted, leaving reproducibility and
comparability in doubt. Moreover, cross-validation protocols and
data partitioning schemes are rarely described, despite their
importance for robust training and unbiased assessment of
models that rely heavily on high-quality data to capture complex, industrially relevant dynamics. To address these gaps, the
community should adopt rigorous information-theoretic tools

Cross validation offers clear advantages—correcting selection

and hyperparameter optimization—an important frontier for
improving both transparency and reliability in hybrid bioprocess

The challenges outlined above often originate in insufficient data
quantity and quality, underscoring the necessity of integrating
hybrid-model data requirements into the experimental design
phase. In this context, Intensified Design of Experiments (iDoE)
offers a compelling solution: by strategically varying inputs and
conditions, iDoE minimizes the total number of trials while maximizing the informational content of each run, thereby furnishing richer datasets that better support the calibration and validation of hybrid bioprocess models [59, 98, 99, 117]. Of course, this
strategy is also limited by monitoring capabilities, since online
data acquisition of primary variables at high frequency still is
a challenge. Developments in process analytical technologies
(PAT) definitely will catalyze the advanced modeling strategies
as hybrid models.

Hybrid Modeling Challenges
Certain challenges for implementing hybrid models have been
mentioned in the literature [26, 55, 264]:
1. The mechanistic part of the hybrid model constrains the
space of solutions obtainable, which helps avoid pitfalls
such as negative concentrations. These constraints impose
an inductive bias into the responses, which might negatively
affect the hybrid model’s performance if the mechanistic
part is not suitable for describing the process.
2. There are standard techniques for identifying parameters
in statistical or purely parametric models. For hybrid models, only a handful of parameter identification methods have
been reported [57, 95, 104, 265]. The major hurdle is the
time needed for parameter identification, due to the extensive calculations that should be performed.
3. In addressing the initial challenge, the integration of hybrid
models requires a thorough examination of the foundational assumptions inherent in the mechanistic knowledge
to be integrated. This task can be approached via two distinct methodologies:

20 of 30
Engineering Reports, 2025
a. The incremental approach, where the most basic
assumptions are made, and more complex interactions
are added until the model performance decreases.
b. The removal approach, where the most complex fundamental structure is evaluated first, and then features are
removed iteratively to determine what part is hindering
the model’s performance.
Both approaches are time consuming, so model development will
require some experience or an analysis of a risk of mechanistic
knowledge being incorrect.
4. Validating and verifying a hybrid model is another challenge, because there needs to be a balance of complexity,
accuracy, interpretability and scalability which is hard to
optimize. Moreover, in hybrid models, nonparametric and
parametric components can introduce distinct sources of
uncertainty and error that must be carefully managed [26].
5. The level of “grayness” in hybrid models—the balance between mechanistic knowledge and data-driven
components—can significantly impact performance. As
illustrated by Rogers et al. [183], incorporating too much or
too little mechanistic knowledge can lead to bias or overfitting, respectively, thus hindering model performance. This
underscores the need for meticulous calibration and validation of hybrid models to ensure optimal balance and performance. Regardless of advancements in key areas, still there
is not a unified framework for determining the valid region
for extrapolation of hybrid models.
Besides the challenges addressed before, we propose the following ones that emerge from the literature review:
1. There
are
no
consumer-ready
applications
built
on
open-source software for building hybrid models easily,
which hinders its adoption by industry, due to the need for
specialized personnel to build, operate and maintain the
models. Although some custom toolboxes for MATLAB like
HYBMOD [125, 220, 222, 233] exist, source code is poorly
documented, and a licensing agreement should be signed.
2. As with many pure data-driven techniques, there is not
a consolidated framework that allows to select the proper
nonparametric technique a priori, meaning that a costly
process of trial and error is necessary to build hybrid models.
3. Like the previous challenge, there is a lack of a general and
unified framework for deciding which type of hybrid model
structure/design pattern is best suited for an application,
which also results in a resource-intensive search.
4. As with many nonparametric techniques, how data should
be split between training, testing and validations has no consensus. Authors commonly only use training and validation
splits due to constraints on the availability of high-quality
data, while few report using datasets for the three purposes.
5. There is no consensus on the training hierarchy of the parametric and nonparametric components of hybrid models.
When using the “delta model” design pattern, the training
of each subcomponent is done separately. However, when

Hybrid Modeling Perspectives
Looking forward, several promising avenues for future research
and development in hybrid semi-parametric modeling are clear.
One key area is the continued refinement of model integration
techniques. Advancements and applications of deep learning
[125, 220, 222] and the development of sophisticated neural network architectures offer opportunities to enhance the nonparametric components of hybrid models. The application of Bayesian
inference, could improve the accuracy and confidence of predictions by incorporating uncertainty quantification into the modeling process [248].
Additionally, expanding the application of hybrid models to
new bioprocesses and products will be crucial. As the bioprocessing industry continues to innovate and develop new products, hybrid models will need to adapt and evolve to meet
these emerging challenges. The growing interest from commercial and industrial sectors, including companies like AspenTech and DataHow AG, as well as the pharmaceutical industry, further underscores the relevance and applicability of hybrid
models in real-world settings. The development of standardized
frameworks and best practices for hybrid model implementation
could facilitate broader adoption and integration into industrial
processes.
Authors should remain open-minded and explore solutions and
implementations beyond hybrid modeling in bioprocesses or
applied mathematics or computer science; for instance, disciplines like agriculture and meteorology have yielded promising
hybrid modeling strategies [268–270]. Although implementations are dependent on data quality and specific to each field,
general insights and strategies can be adapted.
Hybrid semi-parametric models represent a powerful tool for
advancing bioprocess modeling and optimization. Integrating
mechanistic and data-driven approaches offers a pathway to more
accurate, reliable, and scalable models that can meet the complex demands of modern bioprocessing. Continued research and
innovation in this field will undoubtedly unlock new opportunities and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of bioprocesses
across various industries.

Concluding Remarks
This work presents a comprehensive framework for hybrid
modeling in bioprocesses, drawing insights from 270 references. It covers hybrid models’ characteristics, architecture,
and nonparametric structures. Hybrid models are primarily

21 of 30
applied to metabolite production, especially ethanol and penicillin fermentations—followed by cell cultivation and WTT. In
protein production, antibody manufacturing is significant. ANNs
are the dominant nonparametric method, though other ML techniques such as random processes and genetic algorithms are
also used. Most models are trained on experimental data from
laboratory-scale studies, with some full-scale industrial applications. Batch and fed-batch systems are the most common operation modes, while continuous processes are less explored. Frequently used microorganisms include Saccharomyces cerevisiae,
E. coli, and CHO cells. MATLAB is the preferred software, though
Python is gaining popularity due to its robust ML toolboxes.
Finally, while MSE and related metrics are common, no consensus exists on how to best evaluate hybrid model performance.
PSE provides the critical link between these hybrid-model
capabilities and global sustainability imperatives. By embedding
life-cycle
assessment,
techno-economic
analysis
and
multi-objective optimization within hybrid modeling workflows, PSE enables quantitative trade-off studies that reconcile
yield, energy consumption, emissions and cost from early design
through scale-up. Digital-twin simulations and real-time soft
sensors further ensure adaptive control and resilience under
variable feedstocks. Such integrated PSE-driven approaches
directly support UN SDG 7 (clean energy), SDG 9 (industry
and innovation), SDG 12 (responsible production) and SDG
13 (climate action) by valorizing biomass waste, minimizing
environmental impact and fostering low-carbon biomanufacturing. Standardizing PSE-embedded sustainability metrics within
hybrid models will be pivotal for accelerating tangible SDG
progress and closing the financing and implementation gaps that
currently jeopardize the 2030 agenda.

Fermentation optimization is important for industrialization of biological manufacturing, and has been widely
applied to diverse sectors including medicine, food, cosmetics and bioenergy, which is related to substantial
economic beneﬁts. Strain development is considered to be the core part of fermentation technology, as it directly
inﬂuences the product yield and overall success of the fermentation process. However, fermentation design and
process optimization also play a crucial role in fully exploring the genetic potential of engineered strains for
efﬁcient bioproduction. Due to the fact that fermentation process is inﬂuenced by complex factors, so far, machine
learning has been widely used in this area with its strong capabilities of simulation and prediction. This review
provides a brief introduction to the process of fermentation design and process optimization based on machine
learning. In the workﬂow, experimental design strategy is fundamental to explore and characterize the performance of fermentation system. Then, machine learning modelling is employed to simulate the operation of
fermentation system and the appropriate fermentation conditions, such as medium composition and process
parameters, will be determined. Moreover, in recent years, some extension ideas of fermentation design based on
machine learning have also been proposed, including automated fermentation process control, data mining for
exploring strain characteristics, transfer learning, hybrid model building, and soft sensor construction. These
strategies have created more application scenarios for machine learning, enhancing its adaptability in designing
and optimizing the complex fermentation system for efﬁcient bioproduction.
1. Introduction
Fermentation is the process by which speciﬁc metabolic pathways of
microorganisms are utilized to produce metabolites. With the rapid
development of industry, modern fermentation technology enables largescale production of bio-based products. Using renewable substances as
raw materials, fermentation technology contributes to sustainable economic growth, which is beneﬁcial to carbon peaking and carbon
neutrality goals. Strain development is the key issue of fermentation
engineering, but it is also crucial to design and optimize fermentation
process from the perspective of systematic optimization to achieve efﬁcient bioproduction.
In the fermentation process, temperature [1,2], pH [3,4], dissolved
oxygen [5], nutritional conditions (nitrogen source [6], carbon source
[7], mineral salts and vitamins [8]), feeding strategy [9] and other factors will strongly impact the titer and yield of ﬁnal products (Table 1),

between microorganisms and fermentation environment, applying
mechanism models to reﬂect speciﬁc effects of various fermentation

challenge [10]. For example, fermentation kinetics models are mathematical models describing cell growth, substrate utilization and product

the complex internal metabolic processes within organisms and fail to
predict the impact of factors beyond substrate concentration. Therefore,
empirical models are often utilized to represent the input-output relationships between various factors and fermentation results. Empirical
models are black-box models that do not consider the internal mechanisms, and methods of machine learning (ML), a subset of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI), are commonly used to construct such models [12].
ML refers to using empirical data and speciﬁc algorithms on computer

[15] and Artiﬁcial Neural Network (ANN) [16] are typical ML algorithms
for simulating and optimizing the fermentation process. By capturing the
input-output relationship of fermentation system, these models are able
to uncover the complex patterns of interaction and identify optimal
fermentation conditions. In addition, ML methods hold great potential
for modifying metabolic pathways in strains, which can identify potential
overexpression targets for strain engineering [17], screen for the best
combination of biological elements [18], guide the ﬁne tuning of enzyme
levels [19], facilitate de novo promoter design [20], and predict the
impact of 5’ untranslated region on translation efﬁciency [21].
Today, advancements in synthetic biology have accelerated the speed
of strain development and iteration, imposing higher demands on the
efﬁciency of fermentation optimization for newly engineered strains. In
the era of AI, high-performance ML algorithms and high-throughput
fermentation test equipment have been developed, providing impetus
for rapid development in the ﬁeld of fermentation optimization [22].
Some existing reviews have summarized the progress of ML-based
fermentation optimization [23–27]. However, a comprehensive introduction to the overall processes and methodologies involved is still
lacking, and there is no centralized categorization of the extended applications of ML methods in this ﬁeld. To meet these challenges, here we
summarize the algorithms and the concrete workﬂow of ML-based
fermentation design and optimization (Fig. 1), comprising experimental design strategy for fermentation test, ML modeling methods,
model evaluation, hyperparameter tuning and prediction as well as
extension ideas of ML-based fermentation design.
2. Experimental design for fermentation test
Fermentation test serves as a cornerstone for investigating and
characterizing the performance of fermentation system. So far, Onefactor-at-a-time (OFAT) experiments such as removal experiments and
supplementation experiments have been widely used [27], despite being
time-consuming and yielding unstable results. To enhance the effectiveness of fermentation test, a comprehensive process development
strategy has been developed, like DOE (Design of Experiment) strategy
based on statistical principles [28], as depicted in Fig. 2, including
Factorial Design [29], Plackett-Burman Design [30], Orthogonal Design
[31], Uniform Design [32], Central Composite Design [33] and
Box-Behnken Design [34]. The task of DOE can be facilitated by relevant
software, such as Design Expert - a software tailored for experimental
design developed by Stat-Ease, which can generate various experimental
design schemes and conduct basic statistical analysis [35].

Compared to DOE strategy, One-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) experiments
are appropriate in preliminary screening and determining the optimal
level of relatively independent factors [36]. However, the interaction
between different factors cannot be ignored. The primary advantage of
DOE lies in its capacity to evaluate the interactions among various factors
while reducing the number of experiments required. For instance (see
Table 2), Plackett-Burman Design is suitable for preliminary screening of
various factors and identifying dominant ones, which has been widely
used in exploring the effects of mineral salts [37,38]. Orthogonal Design
and Uniform Design are used to assess the correlations among various
factors with different levels [39,40]. Central Composite Design [38,41]
and Box-Behnken Design [42] are specially used for establishing
mathematical relationships between variables and outputs.
In general, when it is not clear which factors have relatively large
impacts on the fermentation results and are most worthy of optimization,
one can start with an Plackett-Burman Design [38], or a Minimum Run
Resolution IV Design [41]. However, these methods cannot quantitatively assess the optimal level of each factor compared to other DOE
strategies. Uniform Design requires relatively less workload, but sacriﬁces a certain degree of accuracy because it does not consider the equal
occurrence of different level combinations. In case of three factors each of
which are to be tested with three levels, Factorial Design, Central Composite Design, Orthogonal Design and Box-Behnken Design require 27,

Therefore, DOE strategy should be reasonably selected according to the
requirements of accuracy and experimental conditions. The selection of
factor levels also signiﬁcantly inﬂuences the validity of the results; thus,
it is essential to have a good understanding of the strain's characteristics
and to consult relevant publications for guidance. What's more, it is
important to note that when testing the inﬂuence of certain factors, it is
necessary to keep other factors at an appropriate level based on
experiences.
Based on DOE, traditional statistical analysis methods such as ANOVA
can be employed to preliminarily assess the impact of various factors and
directly select the best level, but the construction of ML models can yield
more precise predictive results. There is no strict correspondence between speciﬁc ML algorithm and particular experimental design strategy.
Theoretically, different experimental design strategy may be suitable for
different ML algorithms. However, multiple ML algorithms can be
trained on the same set of data, and the best performing model can be
selected afterwards [43]. Data obtained from Factorial Design, Orthogonal Design, Uniform Design, and Response Surface Methodology can all
be utilized for ML model training. Furthermore, we can conduct a new
batch of experiments based on previous experiment, and put them
together for model construction. A typical example is constructing a new
Central Composite Design experiment originating from Factorial Design
[8].
3. Modelling methods for fermentation optimization
3.1. Overview
After obtaining fermentation data, ML algorithms can be employed
for model building to predict the fermentation results under various
conditions. This necessitates a certain level of proﬁciency in mathematical statistics and computer technology. In the age of AI, powerful tools
have emerged, which drastically lower the barrier of usage and facilitate
widespread application of ML across diverse research ﬁelds. Python, as
one of the most popular programming languages for ML, has powerful
packages such as Scikit-learn [44,45]. MATLAB also has a regression
model toolbox containing various ML algorithms [46].
In addition to the algorithm, data quality also represents a critical
factor that impacts the accuracy of the model. Thus, the fermentation
data requires preprocessing before model training [47]. For example,
each feature of data, such as sugar input (g/L) and temperature (C), has
different value range, variance, and unit of measurement. By standardization or normalization, the preprocessed data preserves original characteristics, eliminates inconsistency and enhance model reliability. In the
workﬂow of ML-based fermentation design and process optimization
depicted in Fig. 1, variables involved in fermentation tests are limited
and hypothetically inﬂuential, so the quality of data is only affected by
experimental design and the accuracy of the fermentation result detection. However, if we acquire data from fermentor or even extract
information from the literature, as presented in section 5 (Extension
ideas of ML-based fermentation design), there may be some missing
data or outliers in the dataset. Then, missing value handling and data
cleaning should be applied to enhance data quality.
3.2. Response surface methodology
Response Surface Methodology (RSM) is not a ML method in the
traditional sense, but it also attempts to ﬁnd the relationship between
input variables and output variables. RSM is a simple and effective
modelling method which can be completed by statistical analysis software [48]. Based on the steepness and shape of response surface, it is
possible to observe the inﬂuence of each factor and the interactions. With
regression equation, the optimal fermentation conditions can be predicted [38,41,42,49]. However, the model parameters constructed by
RSM are relatively insufﬁcient. A second-order model only includes the
ﬁrst and quadratic term (x, x2) of each factor, as well as the interaction
term between two factors (x1x2), which lacks the ability to characterize
the complex nonlinear interactions in fermentation system [48].
3.3. Typical ML algorithms
Decision Tree is a ML method based on tree structure [50]. This model
can only predict the approximate range of fermentation result [51].
Random Forests (RF) is an integration algorithm of decision tree with
improved accuracy [14]. By calculating the average of the predictions
from all trees rather than taking the majority vote, Random Forests
Regression (RFR) is capable of addressing regression tasks for fermentation optimization [52]. The advantages of RFR include rapid training

RFR is inevitably inﬂuenced by decision tree partitioning boundaries,
and the predicted fermentation curve presents a discontinuous ladder

Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a popular ML algorithm that uses
hyperplanes to partition the sample space and achieve classiﬁcation of
sample data [15]. The ﬁnal outputs in SVM are heavily inﬂuenced by a
few key samples, indicating that the algorithm possesses not only
simplicity but also robustness. In contrast, Support Vector Regression
(SVR) is a regression algorithm speciﬁcally designed to identify hyperplanes that optimally ﬁt the data [54]. Experimental results indicate that
SVR possesses robust ﬁtting and prediction capabilities especially for a
small amount of data [55]. Therefore, if obtaining sufﬁcient fermentation
data is difﬁcult due to limited experimental condition, SVR can be used
for data ﬁtting and analysis.

multiple neurons to process information [16]. Each neuron receives input
signals from other neurons, combines them based on the weights

used in fermentation optimization (see examples in Table 3), like
Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) [59], Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost)

Vector Machine (LS-SVM) [64,65]. The development of new ML algorithms is always an ongoing process, but the No Free Lunch theorem
states that there is no universal learning algorithm that performs well on
all kinds of tasks [66]. In fact, some algorithms frequently perform better
than others in certain cases. Thus, the understanding of the applicability
of different ML algorithms is beneﬁcial for researchers.
4. Evaluation, hyperparameter tuning and optimal parameters
screening
4.1. Evaluation and hyperparameter tuning
Error is the discrepancy between model prediction and the actual
result, which is utilized to assess the model's capability of ﬁtting and
generalization. Mean Square Error (MSE), Root Mean Square Error
(RMSE), and Correlation Index (R2) are commonly employed for model
evaluation. Different algorithms possess distinct characteristics and
perform well in different tasks, so researchers often train several models
on the same set of data in order to identify the best algorithm [43].
ML models have hyperparameters that determines the model structure as well as the training procedure, which we must set to customize the
model to speciﬁc data [67]. By carefully adjusting hyperparameters, we
will help models to learn universal rules that can be applied to more
potential samples. Tuning hyperparameters manually requires a high
level of expertise from researchers, so automatic hyperparameter tuning
methods, such as Grid Search, Random Search, Bayesian Algorithm and
Genetic Algorithm have been developed. When dealing with models
containing few hyperparameters and only running for a short time,
complex algorithms are often unnecessary. Given that ML models used in
fermentation optimization do not possess a certain level of complexity
and can be ﬁnished within minutes, Huang chose to optimize hyperparameters for RFR, SVR, and BP-ANN models using Grid Search method
to evaluate all combinations of hyperparameters [53].
4.2. Determination of optimum parameters
The main target of incorporating ML models into fermentation process is to identify the optimum parameters, or the combination of factors.
By leveraging ML models to determine the best parameters, higher production efﬁciency can be achieved. While traditional fermentation
optimization focuses on a single production indicator such as titer, we
advocate for the necessity of Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) to
maximize economic beneﬁts. In MMO, a series of objectives are optimized simultaneously based on different levels of importance. For

5. Extension ideas of ML-based fermentation design
5.1. Automated fermentation process control
Fermentation process control is another aspect of fermentation design
and process optimization (Fig. 4a). For example, the feeding rate and
time in batch fermentation have a strong impact on the fermentation
system. Improper feeding strategy can result in starvation, byproduct
accumulation, substrate waste and other issues. Huang et al. developed
an automatic control system for batch fermentation [9], which utilizes an
ANN model to predict glycerol concentration and product concentration
60 min later, with the initial glycerol concentration, the added volume of
glycerol/NaOH and other data as input variables. The system also automatically adjusts the feeding rate to maintain the glycerol concentration
at a low level. This automated system not only eliminates the need for
real-time detection and manual control but also effectively increases 1,
3-propanediol production of C. butyricum while reducing substrate
waste. In addition to the feeding strategy, other process parameters can
be controlled automatically as well. In Mesquita's work, air ﬂow rate was
effectively controlled using an ANN-based micro-aerobic fermentation

5.2. Data mining for exploring strain characteristics
ML is data-driven. After mining relevant data information from
existing publications, models can be constructed to achieve certain predictive functions, providing reference for fermentation optimization
(Fig. 4b). Pensupa et al. conducted data mining on Y. lipolytica and
organized it into a database containing 15 publications [43]. Multiple
regression models were used to accurately predict biomass, with the best
model achieving an R2 value of 0.90. Similar works have been done by
Cos¸gun. Using a dataset containing 356 instances from 22 publications
[51]. Through decision trees, most inﬂuential features that lead to high
biomass production, lipid content and lipid production are identiﬁed. In
order to save manpower and improve efﬁciency, Xiao et al. used the
natural language processing tool GPT-4 to extract information from articles about Y. lipolytica for model training [73]. Random Forests algorithm showed the best performance and predicted the fermentation titers
with high accuracy, reaching an R2 value of 0.86 in test data. In
conclusion, data mining tells us some valuable information about the
characteristics of strains. However, the diversity and heterogeneity of
searched data contribute to limited prediction accuracy, making it
difﬁcult to be applicated in a speciﬁc research of fermentation design and
process optimization.
5.3. Transfer learning
Transfer learning refers to applying knowledge from one task to
another, to enable the adaptation of models trained on large datasets to
new, possibly smaller or more specialized datasets [74] (Fig. 4c). It is a
new breakthrough with the purpose of reducing the number of experiments. Engineered strains with similar physiological characteristics share
some commons during the fermentation process, which is the foundation
of transfer learning. If an existing model has identiﬁed common features
between two systems, it is theoretically possible to be applied to another
system with a small amount of additional data. Huang et al. utilized ANN
for transfer learning in mixed-sugar fermentation [53] and ACSE pretreatment optimization [75]. The Y. lipolytica model constructed by Xiao
et al. also achieved transfer learning on R. toruloides, successfully predicting the impact of gene manipulation on astaxanthin production [73].
However, under normal circumstances, newly engineered strains often
exhibit great changes in metabolic characteristics, posing challenges in
utilizing the fermentation model of one existing strain for transfer
learning into another strain. One potential strategy for enhancing
transfer learning performance is to modularize the transfer model and
separate domain-speciﬁc information from generalizable information
[74]. This can be achieved by employing hybrid models, where a kinetic
model simulates known knowledge and a data-driven model simulates
the unknown part.
5.4. Hybrid model building
The mechanism model is a simulation of the composition and operation of fermentation system, including intracellular metabolic ﬂux and
fermentation kinetics. With the provided initial conditions, these models
are capable of predicting the performance of fermentation system.
However, a single mechanism model is difﬁcult to describe the entire
fermentation process both inside and outside the cell due to the lack of
knowledge, so a hybrid model is constructed with ML as a viable complement [76] (Fig. 4d). For example, omics data reﬂecting the intrinsic
characteristics of strains is now generated at an unprecedented rate but is
hard to be interpreted [77]. Culley's work showed that metabolic ﬂux
omics data and transcriptomics data of S. cerevisiae can be used together
for ML modelling in growth rate prediction [78]. In a previous review,
Wan et al. systematically introduced how omics data are utilized in
process optimization by determining the cell needs during the fermentation process [79]. However, so far, the applications of omics data in
fermentation engineering are still mainly limited to mechanism analysis
for strain development [80–82].
Another example is the combination of ML models and fermentation
kinetics. At the system level, conventional kinetic model is not accurate
enough in predicting fermentation process. However, fermentation kinetics can be used to extract features contained in the fermentation
system and then generate data for ML, making it more robust to the
interference of noise. Lai et al. used generated data from kinetic equations as input to ML models for predicting three off-line parameters and
achieved higher predictive power [83]. Even the parameters of kinetic
model can be estimated with the help of ML. Ismail et al. proposed that
Artiﬁcial Bee Colony and other optimization algorithm can be used for
ﬁtting the simulated model into the experimental data to obtain more
accurate values [84].
In short, integrating ML models with metabolic models may be the
future
solution.
Through
the
simulation
of
genotype-phenotypeenvironment relationships, the reliance on fermentation test data could
be authentically reduced.
5.5. ML-based soft sensor construction
Accurate real-time measurement of key variables is essential for
effective monitoring and control of the fermentation process [85]. Apart
from traditional fermentation sensor, soft sensor has become a new trend.
Soft sensor technology refers to using simple and precise auxiliary variables to calculate other variables that are difﬁcult to measure accurately
and instantly, which is a data-driven process (Fig. 4e). For example,
colors of pH indicator array were used for determination of ethanol
content [86]. Volatile composition of lignocellulosic biomass was used
for estimating cell growth and ethanol production [87]. In comparison,
more auxiliary variables were used by Hua to predict penicillin concentration [88]. Spectroscopic data collected with ATR-MIR was also used
for real-time state estimation based on Partial Least Squares Regression,
then a hybrid model with the kinetic model was constructed and obtained better performance [89]. Certainly, the feature selection of
high-dimensional auxiliary variables is crucial for the development of
soft sensor, and their feature importance must be adjusted before model
training [90]. Another way to improve the robustness of soft sensors is to
utilize transfer learning strategy using data from multiple operating
conditions in different fermentation batches [91]. In conclusion, soft
sensor eliminates the reliance on ofﬂine detection, such as HPLC,
allowing us to easily obtain large amounts of fermentation data. By utilizing these data, it is possible to model the operation of fermentor more
accurately, which could potentially lead to a qualitative leap in feeding
strategy and process control strategy.
Moreover, it is worth noting that biosensors, which are widely used
for screening of high-yield strains, are also potential tools for fermentation process monitoring. Examples include FRET-based lysine biosensor
[92], transcription activator protein-based xylose biosensor [93], transcription factor-based adipic acid biosensor [94] and glycolate biosensor
[95]. For the detection of a single product, biosensors can achieve lower
detection costs and higher throughput than HPLC. However, the fundamental problem with biosensors is that the detection of metabolites is not
real-time, but requires a certain reaction time.
