6. Implementation and numerical experiments
The discretized 1D and 2D governing equations are implemented
and solved in the modular, free and open-source process modeling
software package CADET (von Lieres and Andersson, 2010; Leweke
and von Lieres, 2018). CADET supports several platforms, including
Windows, Linux, and Mac OS. The numerical core is written in C++
and provides a Python interface and frontend. CADET was originally
developed as a fast and accurate numerical solver for mechanistic
modeling in chromatography, including consistent initialization. In
recent years, it has been actively developed and extended to tackle
numerical challenges in other fields. Implementation of the PBM in
CADET has several advantages: 1. CADET supports mathematical models and dedicated solvers for other important unit operations, including
chromatography and filtration. The implemented model family also
covers valves, switches, and tubes to model effects that are external
to the reactor (or column). The output of the PBM can be directly
linked to these units for integrated simulations of processes that consist
of multiple unit operations; 2. Existing infrastructure was reused to
allow, for example, efficient computation of parameter sensitivities via
AD (Püttmann et al., 2013). The Python frontend provides a variety
of tools to solve typical engineering tasks, such as model calibration,
process optimization, and uncertainty quantification. 3. By making the
methods and results of this work publicly available in a continuously
developed and maintained open-source software, it becomes a lasting
contribution.

The error and convergence rate analysis agreed with the above
observation and showed that the upwind scheme demonstrated the
largest normalized L1 norm followed by HR Koren, WENO23 and
then WENO35 for the same 𝑁𝑥. Except for the upwind scheme, a
similar convergence rate of around 2.6 was observed for all high-order
schemes. While the experimental rates for the upwind and WENO23
were easy to explain, the rates for HR Koren and WENO35 were not
within their expected ranges and required further elaboration. There
are several convoluted factors contributing to this observation. First,
for finite volume methods, the convergence rate of the high-order
schemes for the growth flux reconstruction cannot exceed the order of
the boundary treatments. As mentioned in Section 3, the rate of the
high-order schemes were reduced as the lower boundary is approached,
rendering an order of 1 for the first cell. Furthermore, the contribution
of the first cell to the overall convergence rate when increasing 𝑁𝑥is
also reduced, leading to an overall second-order boundary treatment.
Second, the dispersion term was approximated using a second order
approximation. Depending on how strong the growth dispersion is compared with the growth, the overall convergence rate may vary between
2 and the chosen order of the flux reconstruction for the growth which
is again limited by the order of the boundary treatment. In this test, the
expected convergence rate for all high-order schemes is 2. However,
an even better convergence rate of about 2.6 was observed for the
high-order schemes implemented. This indicates that the high-order
schemes were correctly implemented as the design-order discretizationerror convergence is an asymptotic property and represents a lower
bound. Further, the same convergence rate (about 2.4) for the WENO
schemes had also been observed in our previous work (Leweke and
von Lieres, 2018). As seen in Fig. 6(d), the WENO35 scheme not only
could not reach its optimal rate due to the limitations of the boundary
treatment, but also involved more computations which increased its
runtime, making HR Koren and WENO23 the best schemes for this test
case.

and 𝑡= 6 s. To obtain the analytical moments, direct integration
of the analytical solution is difficult. Instead, we used Simpson’s rule

accurate reference values. The relative percent error is presented in
Fig. 3(b). As expected, the zeroth order moment is always accurate,
indicating a correct implementation. The upwind scheme showed the
largest relative error for the sixth order moment, with errors as high as
140%. Overall, high-order schemes worked satisfactorily in capturing
these moments and increased accuracy can be achieved by increasing
𝑁𝑥at the cost of runtime.
6.5. Case 5: isothermal seeded crystallization in a BSTR
In this case, the PBM (Eq. (2)) is coupled to the solute mass
balance equation (Eq. (8)). We assume that the seed distribution is
characterized by a log-normal distribution (52) with 𝑦0 = 0, 𝐴=
1015, 𝑤= 0.3 and 𝑥𝑐𝑒= 40. Unfortunately, an analytical solution is
not available when the mass balance equation is considered. Instead,
reference solutions were obtained using the WENO35 scheme on a fine
logarithmic grid.
Fig. 7(a) shows the results. The green curve is the seed distribution.
The blue curve is the simulated results for an ideal case assuming
that the experimental conditions are carefully designed such that the
particles only grow on the seed and no secondary nucleation occurs.
A unimodal distribution was obtained. Compared with the seed distribution, the final PSD seemed to be narrower due to the scaling on the
logarithmic grid. The orange curve represents a case where unwanted
secondary nucleation occurs, which affects the growth of the seed. A
bimodal distribution was observed as a result of both the growth of
the seed particles and secondary nucleation. The sharp front of the
first mode (counting from left to right) was the result of secondary
nucleation, which decreased rapidly when supersaturation 𝑠decreased
Computers and Chemical Engineering 183 (2024) 108612
due to the solute mass consumed by nucleation and growth, leading
to a classic tailing behavior. The second mode comes from the growth
of the seed particles. Compared to the same mode in the growthonly case, there were significantly fewer large particles. This is not
surprising since a fraction of the total solute mass was transferred to
the first mode. The inset picture depicts the relative supersaturation
𝑠as a function of time: the initial relative supersaturation 𝑠= 0.67
gradually decreased to zero, which stopped further nucleation and
growth. As expected, 𝑠decreased faster when secondary nucleation was
considered.
If the first mode or the secondary particles are undesirable, increasing the amount of seed or using a lower supersaturation helps alleviate
the problem. The blue curve in Fig. 7(b) shows the results obtained
by decreasing the initial supersaturation (𝑠= 0.25). Compared to the
orange curve in (a), which had a supersaturation of 𝑠= 0.67, the height
of the first mode was reduced by a factor of three. Similarly, when the
initial seed amount was quadrupled, the first mode was also substantially reduced in population. In other words, a higher supersaturation or
a lower seed amount induced a stronger or an early onset of secondary
nucleation. This result agreed well with the experimental observations
made by Caillet et al. (2007), Frawley et al. (2012) and Saleemi et al.
(2012).
Further error analysis were thoroughly carried out for three different situations (cases 5A-C). Cases 5A-B considered the growth of the
seed alone on different grid structures. Case 5C considered nucleation
and growth on a logarithmic grid. In case 5 A (Fig. 7(c), (d)) where a
uniform grid was used, the WENO35 performed much better than all
other schemes, exhibiting a convergence rate of 4.7 compared with 0.8,
1.8 and 2.0 observed in the upwind, HR Koren and WENO23 scheme,
respectively. The rates for all the high-order schemes were expected
with the WENO35 approaching its upper bound and the WENO23 lying
on its theoretical lower bound. Since the solution was not entirely
smooth, the HR Koren scheme did not reach its maximum theoretical
rate of 2.
In case 5B ((e), (f)), we are concerned with using a logarithmic
grid structure as the PSD is often reported inherently on a logarithmic
grid by the particle size distribution measurement instrument used.
Compared to the uniform grid case, the experimental convergence rate
for the WENO35 scheme decreased from 4.7 to 3.2, but was still within
the expected range. In contrast, the rates for the upwind, HR Koren,
and WENO23 schemes were slightly increased by about 0.1. Case
5C ((g), (h)) considered nucleation and growth alone without seeds.
Compared with cases 5 A and B, the rates for all high-order schemes
were dramatically decreased with a highest rate of 1.6 observed for the
WENO35 scheme. This was expected as explained in Case 4. With cases
5A-C considered, the WENO35 scheme was the best scheme for this test
case, since its performance always dominated the other schemes ((d),
(f), (h)).
The convergence rates on nonuniform grids in this case were obviously inferior to those attained on uniform grids. This was not totally
unexpected as similar results can be found in the literature. Central
finite volume schemes are known to be only first-order accurate on
logarithmic grids (Turkel, 1986). Wellner also reported a reduced
experimental convergence rate for the WENO schemes on nonuniform
grids for an entropy advection problem (Wellner, 2016). The deterioration might be attributed to the fact that the finite volume scheme is not
generally consistent on nonuniform grids which can lead a reduction
of the rate of discretization error (Diskin and Thomas, 2010; Svärd
et al., 2008). However, a formal and rigorous analysis on the grid
geometry’s impact on the discretization error convergence rate for
high-order schemes is beyond the scope of this article.
Regarding the runtime, there is one interesting note. The logarithmic grid posed a bigger numerical challenge: given the same 𝑁𝑥,
all schemes had much longer runtimes compared to their uniform
grid counterpart (Figure S1(a) and (b)). This is not surprising as the
logarithmic grid has a higher cell density near the lower and middle

WENO23 scheme using the same number of cells 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙. However, it was
surpassed by the WENO23 scheme for errors smaller than about 10−4,
due to the smaller convergence rate of the HR Koren scheme. Taking
the runtime into account, as seen in Fig. 8(c), the HR Koren scheme
was superior to other schemes for a normalized error larger than 10−5,
but was superseded by the WENO23 and WENO35 schemes in an even
smaller error regime.
6.7. Case 7: isothermal continuous precipitation in a DPFR
In this case study we present a test corresponding to the isothermal
continuous precipitation of a solute in a DPFR. The 2D governing
equation (11) is coupled to the solute mass balance equation (15). The
PSD distribution of interest is that obtained at the reactor outlet when
flow equilibrium was achieved. Reference solutions were generated on
a fine grid since there were no analytical solutions available for this
case. Two situations were considered (cases 7A-B): case 7 A assumed
that the particles were born as critical nuclei, and case 7B assumed that
the particles were nucleated with an intrinsic log-normal distribution.
Uniform and logarithmic grids for the internal particle coordinate 𝑥
were tested for both cases. A uniform grid was consistently used for the
external axial coordinate 𝑧. To reduce complexity, the same numerical
scheme was used for the internal and external coordinates, even though
other combinations are generally possible. There are two questions
we want to answer: 1. what is the best scheme for both coordinates
and; 2. what is the optimal trajectory to increase the cell number in
both coordinates to stay on the Pareto fronts? This analysis includes
the normalized L1 norm of the distribution itself and the percent
errors of several scalar metrics. For each scheme in both cases 7A-B,
25 simulations with varying cell numbers in both coordinates were
evaluated on a 5x5 grid. The exact grid arrangement can be found in
Table S10 in the SI.
6.7.1. Case 7A: particles are born as critical nuclei
In case 7 A, particles are born as critical nuclei on a logarithmic
grid. The full 2D-PBM solutions can be obtained at any discrete time
point inside the reactor: Fig. 9(a) shows solutions at 𝑡= 80 s, when
the flow has not yet reached equilibrium and a transient behavior
was observed. The time required to reach flow equilibrium can be
identified by a residence time study, and was found to be about 120 s.
In practice, we are mainly interested in the flow equilibrium solutions
at the reactor outlet, therefore, numerical solutions obtained at 𝑡=
200 s at the outlet were used for further analysis. When comparing
numerical solutions obtained using different numbers of cells in the
axial coordinate 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙, we noticed that a sufficiently large 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙was
crucial for accurate approximations. In Fig. 9(c), an insufficient 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙
led to a truncated intensity of the number density distribution and
over-predictions of the amount of large particles. 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙= 1 and 2 also
presented interesting special cases as the WENO35 scheme was not
fully developed and reduced to the upwind scheme. These cases were
essentially approximations of the DPFR by a single CSTR and two CSTRs
in series, with both having large errors.
Fig. 10 shows the normalized L1 norm vs. runtime. Interpretation
of this figure is similar to those in the 1D cases. However, in the 2D

Moments were used to calculate the volume-averaged mean size,

7. Conclusions
In this article, we solved the population balance model coupled with
a solute mass balance equation formulated for stirred tank and in a dispersive plug flow reactor formats in CADET. We implemented several

W. Zhang et al.
widely-used expressions for the particle nucleation and growth constitutive equations. Due to the open source code of CADET, the mathematical expressions can be modified to accommodate different applications
in different fields which apply population balances. A special population balance formulation that considers the case where the nuclei can
be generated beyond the critical nuclei is also presented. A finite volume method with several flux reconstruction schemes including the upwind, HR Koren with the van Leer flux limiter, WENO23 and WENO35
schemes for arbitrary grids was implemented, and rigorously verified and numerically bench-marked. Analytical Jacobians associated
with all flux reconstruction schemes were derived and implemented to
reduce the runtime.
The fidelity of the numerical representation of each of the terms
of the governing equations was carefully validated throughout seven
test cases. We revisited and improved some of the existing test cases
and generated several new test cases for the 1D and 2D PBM. Novel
bench-marking methodologies were developed to test solver performances. These test cases shed light on appropriate flux reconstruction
schemes and cell numbers to use depending on the chosen crystallization/precipitation mechanisms and initial conditions of the system.
For 1D cases, the WENO35 scheme was observed to be the optimal
scheme to use when there is only growth of an initially smooth particle
size distribution. If the initial distribution is sharp or the particles are
born as critical nuclei, the WENO35 scheme was at best similar to and
sometimes inferior to the HR Koren and WENO23 schemes due to either
increased number of calculations involved or due to limitations of the
boundary treatment. We further found that the use of logarithmic grids
resulted in a higher computational burden and a slower convergence
rate. The former was due to the grid refinement and extra computations
for the scheme coefficients, while the latter might be attributed to the
non-consistency of the finite volume scheme on nonuniform grids.
For 2D PBM cases, we found that an insufficient number of cells
𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙in the external coordinate 𝑧led to under-predictions of the number
density distribution intensity and over-predictions of the amount of
large particles. By examining the normalized L1 norm under different cases, we found that it decreased quickly when increasing 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙,
stressing its importance. Regarding the grid structure for 𝑥, the error
decreased faster on a uniform grid than on a logarithmic grid for 𝑥. This
is because the latter usually had smaller absolute values and errors in 𝑧
were dominant, leading to apparent rate reductions for increasing 𝑁𝑥.
We further found that on a logarithmic grid, increasing 𝑁𝑥and 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙
proportionally helped the scheme to stay on the Pareto fronts. When
increasing 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙and 𝑁𝑥, the runtime increased at a rate of two and one,
respectively. Regarding the scalar metrics, their errors demonstrated
different Pareto optimal behaviors. Sometimes the upwind scheme
could also dominate the performance of high order schemes, but it
would eventually give away if higher accuracy is desired. Errors for the
fine particle count did not converge, possibly due to non-consistency
of the finite volume scheme on nonuniform grids and(/or) a hard grid
search. Overall, a logarithmic grid for 𝑥using the HR Koren scheme and
increasing 𝑁𝑥and 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙proportionally should be the primary choice for
2D cases. However, caution must be taken if the scalar metrics are of
special interest.
The second part of this work was devoted to incorporating the
Smoluchowski equation to account for the aggregation and fragmentation processes in a stirred tank and dispersive plug flow reactor. We
notice that solving the 2D PBM using the finite volume methods has
led to a runtime increase of 1–2 orders of magnitude compared with
1D cases, which can be rather burdensome when solving complicated
optimization problems.
In this work, the external and internal coordinates are discretized
using the finite volume method. This can potentially be improved by
applying high-order methods, such as a non-oscillatory discontinuous
Galerkin method. Previous studies by Breuer et al. (2023) have shown
up to two orders of magnitude of runtime speedup in the external coordinate. As both coordinates can be discretized separately, we expect
Computers and Chemical Engineering 183 (2024) 108612
even greater speedups in the 2D case. The method can potentially be
further improved by concurrently discretizing both coordinates. This
will require substantial changes to the core CADET code and will be
the subject of future work.

A particle size-based Smoluchowski coagulation and fragmentation equation was solved in the free and
open source process modeling package CADET. The WFV and MCNP schemes were selected to discretize
the internal particle size coordinate. Weights in these schemes were modified to preserve and conserve
the zeroth and third moments for size-based equations. Modified propositions and proofs for the scheme
are provided. Analytical Jacobians were derived and implemented to reduce the solver’s runtime. A twodimensional Smoluchowski coagulation and fragmentation equation with axial position as external coordinate
was formulated and discretized to support simulations of continuous particulate processes in dispersive plug
flow reactors. Five 1D and four 2D test cases were used to validate the implementation and benchmark the
solver’s performance. The runtime, L1 error norm, L1 error rate, particle size distribution moments up to sixth
order and several scalar metrics were analyzed in detail.

1. Introduction
The population balance model (PBM) is in wide use for the modeling
of particulate processes including crystallization, precipitation, aerosol
formation, granulation, polymerization, agglomeration and fragmentation. The PBM takes into account important crystallization/precipitation
mechanisms including nucleation, growth, growth rate dispersion, aggregation and fragmentation processes. In part I we solved the PBM
considering nucleation, growth, and growth rate dispersion mechanisms in stirred tank reactors (STRs) and in dispersive plug flow
reactors (DPFRs) (Zhang et al., 2024). The model and algorithm were
implemented and executed in the free and open-source process modeling software package CADET. In part II, we extend the model and
code by incorporating a size-based Smoluchowski coagulation and fragmentation equation to account for particle aggregation and breakage
mechanisms.
The discrete Smoluchowski coagulation equation was originally
proposed by Smoluchowski (1916) to describe the coagulation of colloids that are subject to Brownian motions using a statistical physics
approach. Later, (Müller, 1928) provided a continuous formulation.
The coagulation equation tracks the evolution of the particle number
distribution due to binary aggregation (coalescence, coagulation, agglomeration) processes in which two smaller particles merge into a

larger particle. It presumes that the total volume or mass in the system
is conserved while the particle count is reduced during aggregation. The
fragmentation equation shares the same mathematical origin with the
Smoluchowski coagulation equation but describes the opposed process:
it tracks the evolution of the particle distribution when larger particles
break into smaller particles. It also presumes that the total volume
or mass is conserved, but the particle count increases. Both equations
were originally formulated for one-dimensional (1D) processes in wellmixed batch or continuous STRs. They are not directly applicable to the
continuous two-dimensional (2D) processes that occur in DPFRs.
Mathematically, the governing equations of the Smoluchowski coagulation and fragmentation model are integro-differential equations.
Analytical solutions, when available, are rarely of practical use, as
they require special initial conditions. Various authors have developed
different numerical methods to solve the governing equations. Wellknown solution methods include, but are not limited to, (1) sectional
methods such as the fixed pivot method (Kumar and Ramkrishna, 1996)
and the cell average technique (Kumar et al., 2006), (2) discretization methods such as the finite volume method (Forestier-Coste and
Mancini, 2012; Filbet and Laurençot, 2004; Qamar and Warnecke,
2007; Singh, 2021; Saha et al., 2016; Kumar and Kumar, 2013), finite

W. Zhang et al.
element method (Mahoney and Ramkrishna, 2002) and the discontinuous Galerkin method (Hailiang et al., 2019), and (3) statistical
methods such as Monte Carlo simulations (Eibeck and Wagner, 2000,
2001) and methods of moments including direct quadrature methods of
moments (Marchisio and Fox, 2005) and extended quadrature methods
of moments (Yuan et al., 2012). Among these methods, the finite
volume method (FVM) fully recovers the particle size distribution while
providing a relatively simple mathematical formulation.
In addition to the full distribution itself, higher order moments of
the distribution are of particular interest in many applications since
they represent physical quantities, some of which can be directly
measured using experiments. Moments also provide distribution-related
scalar metrics such as the mean size, total particle count and variance
of the particle size distribution. Moment analysis is frequently used
to evaluate the efficacy of numerical algorithms because higher order
moments are very sensitive to errors in the solution of the governing
equations.
Direct application of the FVM for solving the Smoluchowski coagulation and fragmentation equations is difficult, but highly specialized algorithms have been developed. Based on the FVM, (Filbet
and Laurençot, 2004) have proposed a numerical scheme for the 1D
coagulation equation, which was later extended to higher dimensions
by Qamar and Warnecke (2007). Forestier-Coste and Mancini (2012)
and Filbet and Laurençot (2004) used cell overlapping to formulate
the finite volume preserving scheme that preserves the first order
moment or the total volume on nonuniform grids. This approach was
later applied to a mass-based Smoluchowski coagulation equation and
higher-dimensional cases by Singh (2021). Kaur et al. (2017) formulated a weighted finite volume (WFV) method that preserves the
zeroth and first order moments by introducing two weights in the FVM
discretized source and sink terms. The scheme was shown to provide
shorter runtimes as compared to the FVP scheme for multivariate
aggregation problems. To solve the fragmentation equation using the
FVM, Bourgade and Filbet (2007) proposed a numerical scheme for
binary particle fragmentation with the total volume conserved. To
track multiple fragments, Kumar and Kumar (2013) presented another
scheme to solve a general fragmentation equation that also conserves
the total volume and has second order convergence, independent of
the grid type. Later, both schemes were improved by Saha and Bück
(2021) resulting in much smaller numerical errors for the total particle
count. Saha et al. (2016) introduced the mass conserving and number
preserving (MCNP) scheme on nonuniform grids using two weights in
the discretized source and sink terms. This scheme preserves the zeroth
and first order moments.
In this article, the WFV and MCNP schemes were used due to their
moment preservation and conservation properties and thorough documentation. Additionally, no other higher order scheme with similar
conservation and preservation properties, yet computationally more
efficient, is currently known to us. The WFV and MCNP schemes were
originally derived for the particle volume 𝑣as the internal coordinate, which is a common model when aggregation and breakage are
decoupled from the nucleation and growth mechanisms in the PBM.
However, a formulation based on particle size 𝑥is more convenient
when other mechanisms are also considered in the PBM since the
kinetic expressions for nucleation and growth are often based on particle size. However, only a few articles, published in the 1990s, have
considered the numerical aspects of the size-based governing equations,
e.g. Lister et al. (1995), Hounslow et al. (1988, 2001), Smit et al.
(1994), who used a sectional method to solve the equations.
All model equations and numerical algorithms described here were
implemented and tested in CADET (von Lieres and Andersson, 2010;
Leweke and von Lieres, 2018), a modular, free, and open-source process
modeling software package with a C++ core and a Python interface. CADET comprises a variety of unit operations, including reactors, pumps, valves, tubes, tanks, and uses state-of-art numerical
algorithms and scientific computing techniques to efficiently assemble
Computers and Chemical Engineering 192 (2025) 108860
and solve the underlying differential–algebraic equations. Arbitrarily
many unit operations can be combined, including closed loops and temporal switches, to facilitate integrated process modeling. CADET uses
the backward differential formula (BDF) implemented in the implicit
differential–algebraic solver (IDAS) as time integrator. Application of
the BDF to the size-based FVP and MCNP schemes yields nonlinear
algebraic equations that are solved using Newton iteration. Automatic
differentiation (AD) was implemented in a previous release to provide
the system Jacobian (Püttmann et al., 2016). However, computing and
carrying over the Jacobian in computer memory using AD requires
computational effort and increases runtime. Hence, analytical Jacobians were derived and implemented to reduce computational burden
and enhance solver performance. Optionally, parameter sensitivities
can be computed using different AD techniques, which provide valuable
information and are required for some optimization algorithms when
inverse problems are considered.
The purpose and scope of the work presented here is to: 1. adapt the
WFV and MCNP schemes to size-based Smoluchowski coagulation and
fragmentation equations and; 2. implement, validate and benchmark
the algorithms for the solution of 1D and 2D cases with a particular
focus on the 2D cases, in the free and open-source software CADET.

4. Time integrator
As outlined in Zhang et al. (2024), we use a variable-step/variableorder backward differential formula (BDF) ODE integrator that is implemented in the implicit differential–algebraic solver (IDAS) package in
the suite of non-linear and differential–algebraic equation solvers (SUNDIALS) (Hindmarsh et al., 2005) as the time integrator. During each
time step, a Jacobian matrix is required by IDAS. CADET can generate
this Jacobian using algorithmic differentiation (AD) in forward mode as
implemented in a previous release (Püttmann et al., 2016). However,
repeatedly computing the Jacobian using AD, and storing and carrying
it over in the computer memory slows down the simulations. To reduce
the runtime, we provide the solver with an analytical Jacobian.

As described in case 4 for STR processes, equilibrium solutions occur
only for specific choices of aggregation and fragmentation kernels.

it can be observed depends on several time scales: 1. the time for
the flow to reach the steady state; 2. the time when the observation
is made; and 3. the reaction time required to reach the aggregationfragmentation equilibrium if it exists. There are two requirements to
observe the equilibrium solution at the outlet. First, the reaction time
must be smaller than the time to achieve steady state. Otherwise only

6. Conclusions and outlook
This contribution is an extension to our part I work in which we
solved the PBM in STR and DPFR formats while considering nucleation,
growth, growth rate dispersion, axial convection and diffusion processes in the free and open-source process modeling package CADET. In
this work, we further adapted the WFV and MCNP schemes to discretize
the size-based Smoluchowski coagulation and fragmentation equations
to account for particle aggregation and fragmentation processes. In
addition to their formulation for an STR format, both equations were
also formulated for a DPFR format that included axial convection and
diffusion along the external coordinate.
All equations were implemented in CADET with analytical Jacobians derived and implemented to reduce the computation time. The
implementations were further verified and benchmarked in nine case
studies. The numerical approximations were in excellent agreement

with analytical solutions when available. We observed second order
convergence of the size-based WFV and MCNP schemes on logarithmic
grids for the 1D cases. The second-order rate was attributed to the underlying second-order midpoint quadrature approximation. The zeroth
and third order moments were accurately captured for all 1D cases.
Although preservation of other order moments was not guaranteed
theoretically, they were still approximated with high accuracy.
In the 2D cases, comprising particle processes occurring in the DPFR
format, we compared both the WENO35 and HR Koren schemes as axial
flux reconstruction methods. Both schemes gave similar results in all
cases due to an overall second order convergence rate when combined
with either the WFV or MCNP scheme. After a careful analysis of the
normalized 𝐿1 error and runtime, we found that increasing 𝑁𝑥and 𝑁𝑐𝑜𝑙
proportionally reduced the error most efficiently for a given runtime.
Both the size-based WFV and MCNP schemes were proven to conserve and preserve total particle volume and particle count, respectively. However, these preservation properties depend on the boundary
conditions when combined with other terms in the PBM. We mathematically proved and numerically verified that in 1D cases where
growth and growth rate dispersion are considered, the total count is
still preserved, but the total volume is not strictly conserved. Similarly,
in the 2D cases, where axial convection and diffusion were considered,
all moments were no longer strictly preserved. They are, however, accurate approximations except on very coarse grids. Convergent behaviors
were also observed for their errors.
A future direction would be to provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of the convergence behaviors of the size-based WFV and MCNP
schemes. Moreover, the high-order flux construction schemes could be
modified to force the discretized 1D equations to conserve the third
order moment (Kumar et al., 2013) when combined with growth terms,
and a convergence analysis could be provided for the modified schemes.
Another promising direction is the development of a higher order FEM
to improve computational efficiency. A suitable FEM can be developed
which preserves and conserves the zeroth and third order moments
while retaining higher convergence order. Moreover, a stabilization
mechanism can be considered to adequately resolve steep gradients
when combined with nucleation and growth terms.

A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Precipitation is a valuable alternative to recovery processes like chromatography. While the process is a
plausible alternative, without experimentation, there is a lack of sufficient understanding of how process
operating conditions lead to expected chord length distributions (also referred to as particle size distributions).
In this work, a modeling framework is proposed through which, first, the system is specified, then the
population balance model (PBM) is constructed. Data is then gathered from experiments and subsequently
processed. Afterwards, an optimization problem is defined to regress the PBM parameters to the experimental
data. Finally, a surrogate model correlating the PBM parameters with process operating conditions is developed.
Thereby, avoiding future experiments and regression of the parameters. The application of the modeling
framework is demonstrated using 15 batch experiments for lysozyme precipitation and particle size distribution
measurements using focused beam reflectance measurement (FBRM). The current approach helps identify the
correlations between process operating conditions and process model (PBM) parameters such as maximum
collision efficiency and breakage rate coefficient, which in turn helps in the estimation of the population
distribution in the system. The work also proposes the limitations with modeling and data acquisition that
pave the way for future research.

1. Introduction
Recovery of a biopharmaceutical molecule, such as a protein, usually includes a capture chromatography step, and two chromatographic
polishing steps, followed by ultrafiltration/diafiltration. Downstream
processing is especially significant as manufacturing costs typically account for about 20% of total product sales, with downstream processing
alone representing about 75% of total manufacturing costs (Decker
et al., 2023). To overcome the limitations associated with chromatography (see Fig. 1), such as high costs of resins, diffusion issues, and
capacity constraints, there is a growing interest in exploring alternative
approaches known as ‘‘Anything but Chromatography’’ methodologies (Roque et al., 2020). Currently, nonchromatographic techniques
for downstream processing are experiencing renewed interest, including precipitation methods (dos Santos et al., 2017).
Precipitation can be utilized as a protein recovery method that is
economical, sustainable, and amenable to continuous processing (dos
Santos et al., 2017; Walla et al., 2023), and can produce high yields of
a pure, functional protein. An early demonstration of this principle is
the Cohn precipitation process which is still in use for the separation
of blood products (Cohn et al., 1946). The process utilizes ethanol

and salts, and manipulates pH and temperature to sequentially remove
proteins of therapeutic value from whole plasma (Cohn et al., 1946).
There are two separation strategies available for recovering biologically produced molecules such as proteins, by precipitation. The
first strategy involves precipitating side components, such as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and host cell proteins (HCP), while keeping the
target protein in solution to avoid subsequent protein dissolution and
degradation issues. The second strategy involves using precipitation
to isolate the target protein itself, which is more convenient because
optimal parameters can be selected for one specific target component.
Both strategies involve adding a precipitating agent to the proteincontaining solution. The first strategy causes the impurities such as
proteases (enzymes that break down proteins) to aggregate and become
insoluble, whereas the second strategy causes the protein of interest to
precipitate, while other components remain in the soluble phase. The
resulting protein aggregates can be easily separated from the solution
by centrifugation or filtration. The first strategy is a purification method
while the second strategy is a recovery method. In this work we focus
on recovery. This strategy can significantly enhance the recovery of the
enriched precipitated protein (Burgess, 2009; Gilleskie et al., 2021).

A. Ehtesham et al.
Fig. 1. Overview of the conventional versus alternative purification methods in biopharmaceutical manufacturing.
Precipitation does not require a complex equipment setup compared
to chromatography, a continuous stirred tank (CST) or a tubular vessel
with a filter for solid liquid separation works well. It can deal with
high process volumes and rising titers and can have shorter process
times than chromatography. Furthermore, for applications on a large
scale, the volume of the CST is easily scalable, and continuous operation is feasible (Hammerschmidt et al., 2016; Burgstaller et al.,
2019). Selective precipitation steps can help skipping two of the usual
three chromatography steps, and it is shown that the precipitation
offers cost reductions at all stages of the life cycle of a therapeutic
antibody (Hammerschmidt et al., 2014).
Still challenges to implementation of alternative separation methods in biopharmaceutical manufacturing remain apparent. However,
recent advances in upstream process intensification and adoption of
new technologies enabling continuous manufacturing have successfully increased the titers of even complex molecules like monoclonal
antibodies making these alternative methods potentially more attractive (Müller et al., 2022). There is also a lack of general developmental
knowledge for precipitation processes, and concerns over regulatory
approval due to limited process data generated by the precipitation
process. In this work, we demonstrate a use-case towards recovery of
a selected protein by precipitation, using key factors that affect its
precipitation from the protein solution.
Several factors affect protein precipitation, including pH of the
solution, salt concentration, temperature, agitation, protein concentration, presence of co-solvents, and buffer solutions. Variation in pH
impacts protein solubility and precipitation by altering the charge
distribution on the protein surface. Salt concentration and salt type,
as outlined in the Hofmeister series, significantly influences protein
stability and solubility due to ions kosmotropic or chaotropic properties. Temperature affects the balance between hydrophobic interactions
and other forces that maintain protein solubility. Agitation improves
precipitation efficiency by promoting the mixing of precipitants into
protein solutions and increasing the probability of collision (Sommer
Computers and Chemical Engineering 200 (2025) 109193
et al., 2015). Protein concentration determines the solubility limit and
the likelihood of precipitation (Burgess, 2009). The presence of cosolvents and buffering agents also affects protein solubility and impacts
interactions crucial for protein precipitation (dos Santos et al., 2017).
These factors such as salt and protein concentration, agitation, etc.,
collectively shape the outcome of protein precipitation processes by
modifying solubility, stability, and protein–solution interactions and a
unique set of values of these factors will affect proteins in a different
way.
1.1. Batch processing and monitoring solutions
Despite the inherent simplicity of batch processing, no established
standard for protein precipitation conditions currently exists, primarily because the unique and complex structures of individual proteins
lead to distinct biological characteristics. These processes are highly
sensitive to various inputs, such as shear forces, salt concentration,
and protein concentration. Altering any of these parameters can significantly impact the success of protein recovery by precipitation.
Therefore, precise control of process operating conditions is crucial for
the successful execution of these processes.
Focused Beam Reflectance Measurements (FBRM) and in situ microscopy via Process Video and Measurement (PVM) microscopes are
available tools for monitoring precipitation and crystallization operations (Zhang et al., 2024; Walla et al., 2023). In situ monitoring
tools are increasingly preferred because of their ability to provide
near real-time information without the delays and additional labor
associated with ex situ particle analysis techniques. Additionally, in situ
methods help mitigate potential artifacts caused by sample preparation,
such as changes in precipitate conformation due to dilution or alterations in ionic strength that is often necessary for at-line or off-line
sampling. Modern advances allow for the analysis of larger particle
populations using near real-time particle imaging techniques. These
methods typically involve capturing images with a confocal microscope

A. Ehtesham et al.
and highspeed camera, followed by processing with segmentation algorithms to identify and extract various particle properties for each
particle (Patchigolla and Wilkinson, 2009). Although techniques such
as laser diffraction or electrical sensing zones may not be suitable to
accurately determine particle size and shape distribution, microscopy
coupled with image analysis, whether ex situ or in situ, is widely
used (De Anda et al., 2005).
FBRM provides the chord length distribution (CLD) of a particle population, operates by analyzing back-scattering from a rotating
monochromatic laser beam. Its ability to function even in concentrated
slurries eliminates the need for additional dilution steps or external
sampling, making it suitable for online monitoring. However, the effectiveness of FBRM is highly dependent on the optical properties of the
surfaces of the particles. It provides highly sensitive real-time tracking
of particle size, number, and shape changes without the need for offline sampling. It also detects key process events such as nucleation,
growth, and dissolution, for fingerprinting particle system distributions. However, its ability to directly track crystal size is limited to
spherical crystals, as the measured CLD corresponds directly to the
crystal size distribution (CSD) only in these cases. For non-spherical
crystals, mathematical corrections are required to convert CLD data
into CSD, which remains a significant challenge. Despite ongoing research to refine these conversion algorithms, this limitation remains a
drawback of FBRM technology (Zhang et al., 2024). Although FBRM
is well established for monitoring small molecule crystallization, its
application to biological macromolecules like proteins remains limited,
with only a few publications exploring its potential in this area (Walla
et al., 2023). Combining PVM with FBRM enables the differentiation
of precipitate identity (De Anda et al., 2005). For example, PVM can
be used to differentiate bubbles, oils, and protein crystals that will
contribute to the CLD regardless of their identity. PVM also provides
turbidity information that can pair well with chord length distribution
to fully describe the stages of a precipitation process (De Anda et al.,
2005).
1.2. Modeling approaches
Modeling plays a crucial role in understanding the fundamentals
of a system (Pistikopoulos et al., 2021; Mansouri et al., 2025). While
empirical data helps detail observations from the phenomena, models
are used to approximate and predict system behaviors that are difficult
to measure. Validated models, by simulating processes, help reduce
costs by minimizing the need for extensive and time-consuming physical experimentation. Utilizing models can enhance quality control by
helping to understand the relationship between process variables and
product quality, enabling better control over manufacturing processes.
Certain fields, such as chemical engineering, rely on fundamental principles like conservation laws, contrasting with the widespread use of
data-driven or black-box modeling in areas like image recognition and
natural language processing (Chakraborty et al., 2022). A purely blackbox approach may struggle to generalize to unseen data and risks
overfitting, while a strictly mechanistic model faces challenges due to
the many variables and parameters that are difficult to measure or
estimate (Chakraborty et al., 2022). Therefore, there is an interest in
research to develop data-driven models and combining them with first
principles/mechanistic knowledge.
The combination of mechanistic models and machine learning (ML)
models is pivotal in protein precipitation, merging mechanistic models
for the phenomenology, and data-driven methods to enhance prediction accuracy and parameter estimation. This integration is crucial in
process and product engineering, providing adaptable, reusable, and
predictive frameworks for addressing complex challenges (Mansouri
et al., 2025). In pharmaceutical production, where process optimization
and shortened development cycles are paramount, this hybrid modeling
approach offers numerous advantages. The ability of this approach to
assimilate various knowledge sources, including prior information and
Computers and Chemical Engineering 200 (2025) 109193
data-driven insights, makes it adaptable to diverse processes and complexities. Leveraging these models combining first-principles/mechanistic knowledge with data from experiments in protein precipitation
facilitates parameter optimization and enables the prediction of particle
size distribution and agglomeration dynamics during precipitation. This
results in increased process efficiency, reduced costs, and improved
product quality by tackling operational challenges, optimizing parameters, and making informed decisions based on system understanding
and data-driven insights. For more information around this topic, we
guide the readers to the following papers, Schubert et al. (1994)
and Zhao et al. (2023) for a detailed explanation of using hybrid
modeling, particularly in yeast fermentation processes. We would also
like to draw attention to Hamilton et al. (2017) that developed hybrid
models for predictions of a class of dynamical systems, and Nielsen
et al. (2020a), Nielsen et al. (2020b) that used a hybrid model predictive control strategy for particle processes such as crystallization,
flocculation or precipitation.
Combination of mechanistic models and ML models have been
utilized in flocculation and related processes to predict kinetics and
process parameters (Nielsen et al., 2020a; Nazemzadeh et al., 2021),
assist in optimization, and aid in the development of soft sensors and
process control (Nielsen et al., 2020a; Boskabadi et al., 2025, 2024).
Several structural approaches exist in the literature for combining
mechanistic models and ML models, either in parallel or in series, to
improve process modeling.
In this work we have adapted a systems approach to model protein
precipitation using lysozyme as a model product. The approach is capable of being applied to similar protein systems, both in the population
balance modeling (PBM) (to estimate the particle size distribution from
the PBM parameters) and in the surrogate modeling/ML methods (to
correlate the PBM parameters to process operating conditions) to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the precipitation dynamics of batch proteins (Nielsen et al., 2020a). Furthermore, Samad et al.
(2011) developed a generic multi-dimensional model for batch cooling crystallization, and Meisler et al. (2014) modeled crystallization
kinetics with a generic modeling framework.
The manuscript is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the
modeling framework with details on the population balance model
and empirical correlations that estimate the particle-size distributions
from operating parameters. The details of the surrogate model (using
ML) to correlate the PBM parameters against the process operating
conditions for fast estimation of PBM parameters, are also mentioned
in this section. Section 3 provides details of the experimental procedure
and data acquired from the process, using the FBRM probe as well as
the experimental setup. Section 4 presents results from the application
of the modeling framework to the case of precipitation of lysozyme (as
described in Section 3). It also shows how the framework is used for the
estimation and prediction for the particle-size distribution, sensitivity
with changing PBM parameters, and predictions of the PBM parameters
from the process operating conditions via a surrogate model. We also
showcase in this investigation the limitations to further future research.
2. Modeling framework
The goal of this work is to obtain a dynamic model to predict precipitation of a specific product at different process operating conditions.
With limitations on the exact know-how to aid in this estimation of
the process dynamics, we have envisioned a framework that combines
the population balance model (PBM) for protein precipitation, with a
surrogate model for estimation of critical parameters in the PBM. Towards this goal, first, the PBM parameters are regressed based on each
experimental dataset of particle size distribution, and subsequently, the
surrogate model is trained to predict the regressed PBM parameters as
a function of the process operating conditions. The surrogate model
can then be used to predict the PBM parameters directly from the
operating conditions, which can then be used to predict the particle
size distribution (PSD) using the PBM model. Fig. 2 shows the detailed
overview of the modeling framework. In the following sections these
steps are explained in detail.

A. Ehtesham et al.
Fig. 2. Modeling framework overview.
2.1. Step 1: System specification
To design an efficient protein precipitation process, it is essential
to understand the system and develop predictive models that can save
both time and costs. We first chose a known and robust protein precipitation system to generate data for modeling. Then, a mechanistic model
is employed to provide accurate predictions of the system’s behavior.
In this work, a one-dimensional PBM is used as the mechanistic
model to predict the dynamics of the precipitation process. Different
phenomena and mechanisms can lead to the birth and death of particles. These phenomena include agglomeration, growth, nucleation,
shrinkage and breakage, etc. The PBM contains parameters that will be
discussed later and are either difficult to measure or estimate. ML methods can be used to assist in estimating these parameters. It is assumed
in this study that only agglomeration and breakage phenomena are
present, the effects of nucleation and growth are neglected. At the start
of the experiment, all particles are assumed to be primary particles,
as lysozyme crystals are initially seeded into the solution, thus the
assumption of no nucleation. Multiple coefficients are employed within
the equations to characterize the interrelations within the system.
The PBM considered in this study is one-dimensional, describing the
evolution of the mean chord length of protein precipitates as measured
by FBRM. The model includes agglomeration and breakage phenomena
in a single dimension, as this is sufficient to capture the primary
dynamics of the system without introducing unnecessary complexity. A
one-dimensional PBM is justified because the objective is to model the
dynamic changes in chord length distribution rather than tracking the
full particle size distribution. While a higher-dimensional PBM could
provide more detailed insights, the available measurement technique
(FBRM) primarily provides chord length distributions, making a 1D
representation the most practical choice.
2.2. Step 2: Model construction
The model structure is envisioned as a two module system, that (1)
estimates the particle-size distribution given the PBM parameters, and
(2) correlates the process operating conditions with PBM parameters
using a surrogate model.

• Perikinetic agglomeration: This process involves the agglomeration of particles due to their random motion, known as Brownian
motion. Brownian motion is characterized by the random and
chaotic movement of particles or molecules, which is highly influenced by the system’s temperature. It becomes notably slower
for particles larger than 1 μm and can generally be disregarded
for larger particles.
• Differential sedimentation: The motion of particles in vertical
and in the direction of the bottom of the vessel. The settling
velocities of particles would be different based on the difference
in their size and densities.
• Orthokinetic agglomeration: Also known as shear-induced agglomeration, this mechanism occurs due to the movement of particles induced by velocity gradients within the system, typically
generated by impellers inside the Vessel. It finds extensive applications across various industrial processes. The shear and mixing
created by these velocity gradients lead to a higher frequency of
collisions between particles. Additionally, it is important to note
that increased shear can also enhance the breakage of weakly
attached particles.

2.3. Step 3: Data acquisition
The data acquired in this work are the process operating conditions
and the output chord-length distribution (also referred to as PSD),
for each operating condition. The chord-length distribution is usually
collected with a given frequency which needs to be provided to the
model, during the optimization state of the problem.
Data for chord-length distribution is observed as the number of
particles of a particular size as seen by a sensor of choice. These are
often paired as ({𝐿𝑖, 𝑁𝑖,𝑡}) where 𝐿𝑖 is the chord-length and 𝑁𝑖,𝑡 is the
number of particles recorded by the sensor at time 𝑡, for chord-length
𝐿𝑖. The resultant data acquired is a multidimensional time-series.

2.4. Step 4: Data preprocessing
The data acquired is converted to a chord-length distribution based
on the discretized scheme, this means that the measurements are put
into their respective particle size bins made in the discretization step
to ensure the same resolution with the modeling results.
These distributions are then normalized to preserve the dynamic
characteristics of the system and ensure consistency across different
experiments and simulation runs. The normalization step is crucial, as
it aligns the scale of experimental observations with that of the model,
particularly in terms of particle population, making the comparison
between the two meaningful and accurate. Additionally, this transformation enables interpolation across chord-length ranges that may not
have been directly captured during the measurements, allowing for a
more continuous and representative distribution to be used in model
evaluation.
To ensure numerical stability and robustness during the simulation
and optimization, further preprocessing is applied. Negative values in
the simulated outputs are removed to maintain physical realism, and
a minimum threshold is imposed to prevent division by zero during
subsequent calculations. Both simulated and experimental distributions
are normalized into probability distributions by dividing each by their
total particle count.
2.5. Step 5: PBM parameter (𝛼𝑚𝑎𝑥 and 𝐸) identification
In this study, we consider agglomeration and breakage to be the
primary phenomena governing the precipitation process. A PBM was
developed based on these phenomena to predict the system’s dynamics
over time. The PBM predicts particle length distributions for each
experiment, with model parameters influencing the kinetics of precipitation.
For each experimental dataset, the counts of measured chord lengths
are redistributed into the corresponding PBM bins by summing the
contributions of data points that lie within each bin’s boundaries. This
ensures that the measured distributions are represented at the same
resolution as the PBM, allowing for direct comparison and integration
into the modeling framework.
The objective function for the optimization has to represent the
similarity between the predictions and the measurements. Although
several objective functions can be defined and would all work, using a simpler and more efficient approach enhances computational
speed. Therefore, instead of complicating the objective function, the
KL divergence between predicted values and measured values has been
chosen as the objective function. The use of KL divergence in the
context of protein size distributions has already been reported in the
literature (Maddux et al., 2017).
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence is a measure of how one distribution diverges from a second, reference distribution. It quantifies the
difference between the simulation distribution 𝑃𝑖 and measured distribution 𝑄𝑖. Mathematically, KL divergence is not symmetric, meaning

2.6. Step 6: Surrogate development and application
A key problem to be addressed by the framework is to correlate
the PBM model parameters, specifically 𝛼max and 𝐸, with the process
operating conditions. To correlate the process operating conditions to
the parameters of the PBM, a surrogate model is required that can
adequately estimate these PBM parameters.
In our case, an artificial neural network-structure with 1 inputlayer with 4 inputs (corresponding to the process operating conditions),
1-output layer with 2 outputs (corresponding to 𝛼max and 𝐸), and 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons and 32 neurons, respectively, was used. The
model has in total 3 layers apart from the input layer, with a ReLU activation function after each layer. Implementing dropout layers helps the
model by reducing over-fitting. The neural network architecture was
built using the PyTorch module on Python. Supplementary material
(Table S4) provides more details about the neural network structure.
Details on training are elucidated in Step 6: Surrogate development and
application.
The surrogate model is structured to take the process operating
conditions, such as protein concentration, salt concentration, rotation
speed, and temperature for each experiment as inputs, to predict the
PBM parameters (𝛼max and 𝐸) for each experiment. Given the computational cost to predict the PBM parameters for each individual
experiment, and the experimental effort to collect the process operating
conditions data alongside the PSD, a surrogate model is required to correlate the process operating conditions to PBM parameters, for better
design of experiments. This trained model can be used to predict the
optimized 𝛼max and 𝐸, obtained after step 5. To correlate the process
operating conditions to the optimized parameters of the PBM, any ML
model may be used.
Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function and Adam optimizer are
used to train the surrogate model that correlates the process operating
conditions to PBM parameters. The MSE loss calculates the average
of the squares of the differences between the predicted and actual
PBM parameter values (which are obtained post-optimization in step
5), inherently penalizing larger errors more significantly; this quality
makes it especially suited for regression tasks where precise numerical
predictions are crucial.
Since the number of samples is minimal, it was decided to use crossvalidation and training to improve the regularization of the model.
The model was trained on 10,000 epochs to ensure sufficient learning.
The neural network’s loss optimizer used mean squared error between
the predictions and the training values as the objective function. More
information is given in the supplementary material (Section S6). At
the end of step 6, we have successfully obtained PBM parameters,
i.e., the regressed PBM parameters for each experiment. We have a
surrogate model that can predict the regressed process parameters from
the process operating conditions.

3. Lysozyme precipitation: Experimental setup
We chose a simple and robust protein–buffer system of lysozyme
in sodium acetate pH 4.0 to demonstrate the usefulness of process
analytical technologies. At low pH, lysozyme is highly charged and
will not interact with itself in solution. The addition of salts like
sodium chloride influences precipitation by modifying interactions,
with the rate depending on solution molarity. This well-characterized
crystallization system of lysozyme in sodium acetate pH 4.1 buffer was
chosen as a starting point for developing a robust precipitation system
which preserves functional proteins (Judge et al., 1999). Lysozyme has
a pI value of 10.7, and is therefore expected to be fully charged at pH
4.1 (Baron et al., 2016). The published lysozyme sodium acetate with
NaCl process produced tetragonal crystals without shear, suggesting
that the interaction kinetics were amenable to a controllable precipitation process. Shear was added to test precipitation kinetics at various
protein, salt, temperature, and agitation rate combinations.
The 0.1 M sodium acetate pH 4.1 solution was made in deionized
water and adjusted to pH 4.1 with glacial acetic acid. The reported
buffering capacity of sodium acetate is pH 3.6 to 5.6. Lysozyme and
NaCl were combined in the base sodium acetate buffer. All solutions
were filtered through a 0.1 μm filter prior to vessel addition.
Precipitation screening was achieved by adding increasing amounts
of salt and protein and reacting overnight at 25 ◦C at a moderate
shaking speed in a 96-well format (cat. 3788, Corning) and using binary
well scoring for visible precipitation.
3.1. Process analytical technology
Dynamic light scattering
To monitor sub-visible particle–particle interactions, dynamic light
scattering (DLS) with the DynaPro Plate Reader III™ (Wyatt Technology) was used to identify the appropriate buffer range and determine
aggregation propensity in solution at low to modest NaCl concentration
in 96-well batch format (cat. 3603, Corning).
Process analytical technology
To monitor the precipitation process, a Mettler Toledo EasyMax
102 workstation with a 100 mL vessel was setup with a five-port
headplate. The EasyMax workstation provides temperature and agitation process control and syncs with the process monitoring probes.
The stirring crossbar configuration was chosen to accommodate the
necessary probes. The focused beam reflectance measurement (FBRM)
G400 probe and the EasyViewer 100 probes were submerged in the
vessel. The FBRM measures CLD and particle counts. The EasyViewer
monitors turbidity and records particle images. Data collection from
both the FBRM and the EasyViewer was done in the iControl software.
The probes were submerged in the lysozyme only solution to establish a baseline. The NaCl solution was added ten minutes after lysozyme
and the entire precipitation was monitored for 24 h.
EasyMax 102
The experiments in this study were conducted on an advanced synthesis workstation, EasyMax 102, from Mettler Toledo. A 100 mL glass
vessel attached to a temperature probe, FBRM probe, Turbidimeter, and
magnetic stir bar is utilized as shown in Fig. 5. A deep vortex is created
by the use of a magnetic stir bar. Temperature is maintained at a set
point by a water-cooled jacket. An overview of the experimental setup
is provided in the supplementary material (figure S1).

A FBRM (focused beam reflectance measurements) model G400
Mettler-Toledo probe was used for this study. The instrument ParticleTrack G400 uses an FBRM probe-based technique. A rotating
monochromatic laser beam is used to analyze backscattering, and
FBRM can be used even in concentrated slurries. A particle’s optical
properties play a crucial role in FBRM since it is based on scattered
laser light reflection on encountered particles in the system. The
instrument is inserted at an angle into the process stream to ensure

To focus a laser beam on a narrow spot at the sapphire window,
a set of optics is placed down the probe tube. By rotating the optics
at a fixed speed, typically 2 m/s, the beam spot rapidly scans across
particles as they pass the window. The laser beam scans throughout
the particle system, and as it reaches an individual particle or more,
the laser light will be backscattered to the detector. When the focused
beam reaches a particle, the laser light reflects to the detector. These
pulses of backscattered laser light are counted, and the particle distance
is determined by multiplying the duration of each pulse by scan speed.
The particle distance known as the chord length is a fundamental
measurement of particle size.

of mechanistic model quality and information available for model training, that is typically expressed as the
amount of data available. While hybrid models – which integrate mechanistic and data-driven components –
have gained significant attention in process systems engineering, their advantages over purely mechanistic or
data-driven alternatives remain inadequately quantified. We address this gap by investigating two critical fac­
tors: (i) the impact of mechanistic model fidelity on hybrid model performance, and (ii) the influence of cali­
bration dataset size on prediction accuracy. Our methodology is validated through an in-silico case study of
baker's yeast cultivation and a real-world industrial application of ion-exchange chromatography in biophar­
maceutical manufacturing. Results demonstrate that hybrid models consistently outperform purely mechanistic
and data-driven approaches when the mechanistic component captures fundamental process behaviours, even
with structural simplifications. Notably, hybrid models maintain superior predictive capability in extrapolative
scenarios; however, when mechanistic knowledge is severely limited and insufficient information is available for
compensation, hybridisation benefits diminish substantially. The work provides quantitative guidance for
practitioners to determine when hybrid modelling represents a justified investment of modelling resources in
process engineering applications.
1. Introduction
In recent years, a variety of modelling approaches have gained sig­
nificant attention to support the design and optimisation of engineering
processes across diverse industrial sectors (Zhang et al., 2019). The
growing interest in adopting mathematical models is motivated by the
increasing demand for more efficient and reliable approaches to process
development and decision-making, especially in contexts where experi­
mental campaigns are costly, time-consuming, or limited by operational
constraints (Wang et al., 2024). The level of knowledge and understanding
of the process, as well as the amount of information required for cali­
bration and validation of a model at a given stage of process development,
can vary significantly, affecting the selection of the modelling method
(Chen and Ierapetritou, 2020; Zendehboudi et al., 2018).
Depending on the extent of the underlying physics that is captured by

into three main types (Bonvin et al., 2016; Moser et al., 2020): mecha­
nistic models (also referred to as knowledge-driven, first-principles, or
white-box models), data-driven models (often called empirical or
black-box models), and hybrid models (also known as semi-empirical or
grey box models). One of the primary benefits of mechanistic models is
their ability to enhance understanding of products and processes by
explicitly describing the physical, chemical, and biological properties of
the system under investigation. They typically require few calibration
experiments and provide superior extrapolation capabilities compared
to data-driven approaches. However, deriving their equations may be
complex, as it involves identifying the exact underlying physical phe­
nomena that characterize the process under analysis, and demands more
time, resources, and modelling effort, often requiring high computa­
tional burden (Solle et al., 2017). In cases of limited knowledge and

process understanding, a mechanistic modelling approach may be
insufficient to reliably enable simulation-based development and opti­
misation, often resulting in process-model mismatch, i.e., a discrepancy
between predictions and experimental data.
On the other hand, empirical models only rely on available historical
data. The main advantages include their ability to capture correlation
structures within data with no need of detailed understanding of the
underlying physics, rapid development timelines, and reduced compu­
tational demands, particularly when they offer simplified representa­
tions of highly complex mechanistic models (Reis and Saraiva, 2019;
Rendall and Reis, 2018). Nonetheless, they typically require extensive
calibration datasets, which may be limited or inconsistent in terms of
structure and quality. Furthermore, generalization and interpretability
can be more challenging since their performance may strongly reduce
when applied to explorative scenarios (Sansana et al., 2021).
When tackling real-world problems, all available sources of infor­
mation (i.e., physical understanding of the system and historical process
data) should be leveraged. In this context, hybrid modelling strategies
are effective alternatives aiming to integrate the physical knowledge
embedded in the available mechanistic model with empirical data (von
Stosch et al., 2014). As a result, hybrid configurations preserve core
insight into the underlying physical process mechanisms while extract­
ing information from available data-driven patterns that cannot be
captured by first-principles knowledge, thereby enhancing both pre­
dictive accuracy and interpretability (Sansana et al., 2021). Addition­
ally, hybrid models can contribute to reducing the overall time required
for model development. In general, extending a mechanistic model to
include more detailed knowledge can be a time-consuming task
(Schweidtmann et al., 2024). By leveraging the flexibility of data-driven
components, part of the knowledge not explicitly captured in the
mechanistic equations can instead be extracted by appropriately
modelling the available process data, thereby accelerating the con­
struction of reliable process models.
Over the last years, various studies have explored the potential of
hybrid models across different domains. For instance, Sch¨afer et al.
(2019) used artificial neural networks combined with differential
equations to model rectification columns, and the model was later used
for real-time applications (Lüthje et al., 2021). Bui et al. (2021) pro­
posed a hybrid model configuration combining a fundamental adiabatic
reactor model with an empirical partial least-squares regression to
monitor and predict the catalyst lifetime of an operating industrial
reactor. Shah et al. (2022) demonstrated the high predictive capability
of a deep neural network-based hybrid model for an industry-scale
fermentation process, outperforming a purely mechanistic kinetic
model. Polak et al. (2023) developed a hybrid modelling approach to
evaluate the effects of raw material variations and process parameter
fluctuations on product quantity and quality in a flow chemistry process
for small molecules manufacturing. Xie et al. (2024) employed a neural
network to compensate for the unmodeled dynamics of the
first-principles model on an industrial nitration process under
load-changing scenarios. Mahanty et al. (2025) proposed a hybrid model
to predict diesel fuel removal dynamics, with the instantaneous removal
rate modelled using an artificial neural network. Michalopoulou and
Papathanasiou (2025) integrated artificial neural networks with process
knowledge to describe the nonlinear dynamics of a chromatographic
separation process. Caspari et al. (2025) provided evidence that hybrid
models remain effective in data-scarce scenarios, highlighting their
robustness with limited information. Steinacker et al. (2025) explored
the potential of hybrid models based on different neural networks and
compared the performance to typically used mechanistic models to
predict atypical trajectories of hematotoxicity damage to chemotherapy
patients. Wang et al. (2025) demonstrated the improved performances
of physics-data-driven hybrid models to predict accurately the friction
torque in hydraulic motors.
However, not only do hybrid models require a careful integration of
system knowledge and historical data, but they also necessitate a deep
understanding of when and how each component of the model (i.e., the
mechanistic and data-driven ones) can contribute to the overall hybrid
performance (Rogers et al., 2023; Bradley et al., 2022). Developing a
comprehensive framework to systematically construct and integrate
these components remains challenging (Shah et al., 2024). This repre­
sents a clear need for further development to ensure that hybrid ap­
proaches can be more systematically and effectively applied in process
engineering (Schweidtmann et al., 2024). Most published contributions
analyzing how the quality each component or the limited amount of
information available for model training impact on the overall hybrid
model performance are based on synthetic or simulated datasets, with a
notable lack of studies addressing real-world processes in a generaliz­
able framework. These works are also generally limited to specific ar­
chitectures (Narayanan et al., 2022).
Our methodology is designed for cases in which models are developed
for offline analysis and optimization purposes, such as for process design,
scale-up and simulation. While several studies have explored hybrid
modelling architectures and performance metrics, most contributions do
not quantify the relative impact of mechanistic accuracy and data avail­
ability on the predictive reliability of hybrid models. This work specif­
ically addresses this gap by analysing how these two factors interact and
affect model robustness under both in-silico and industrial conditions.
Our investigation encompasses both in-silico and real-world case
studies. Specifically, an in-silico study conducted on a fed-batch reactor
system for baker’s yeast production is used to address key challenges,
such as the limited predicative capability of available mechanistic
models and the paucity of data, and questions the effectiveness of hybrid
modelling under such constraints. An additional in-silico case study
concerning urethane synthesis is presented in the Supplementary Ma­
terial. Finally, a real-world case study concerning ion-exchange chro­
matography in biopharmaceutical manufacturing aims at providing
insights concerning typical challenges in industrial applications.
The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe the
general methodology for the analysis and construction of suitable hybrid
modelling configurations. In Section 3, we give details about the in-silico
and real-world case studies, respectively. Results are presented and
critically discussed in Section 4. Final remarks conclude the manuscript.
2. Methodology
2.1. General methodology
The methodology is structured into a sequence of steps, each of them
contributing to the systematic construction and evaluation of suitable
hybrid models (Fig. 1). Here, we aim to assess: (i) the impact of different
levels of complexity in the mechanistic component, and (ii) the effect of
the amount of information available on the overall hybrid model per­
formance. These aspects are crucial to evaluate the robustness and
generalization capabilities of the methodology under various practical
scenarios. The methodological steps are outlined in Fig. 1.

provide an approximate representation of the system under investiga­
tion, based on the modeler's prior knowledge. In mathematical terms,
the relationship between the process inputs and outputs can be

2.1.2. Step #2 – construction of hybrid model
While mechanistic models offer a structured and interpretable
description of the underlying physical and chemical phenomena, they
often suffer from structural inaccuracies due to simplifications,
unmodeled dynamics, or missing mechanisms. To account for processmodel mismatch, a hybrid modelling structure that integrates a datadriven component into the mechanistic framework can be used. Spe­
cifically, we propose an architecture where the mechanistic component
provides initial predictions of the states and outputs of the system
(Sansana et al., 2021); The data-driven component takes the mechanistic
component outputs, along with the experimental inputs available, and is
constructed to model the estimation error of the mechanistic compo­
nent, thus compensating for the observed mismatch (Fig. 2).
The proposed architecture differs from the typical serial or parallel
configurations reported in the literature (Sch¨afer et al., 2020; Shah et al.,
2024). It combines elements of both approaches: similar to parallel
structures, the data-driven component corrects the output of the
mechanistic model by compensating for its systematic deviations. At the
same time, it shares a feature with serial structures, since the data-driven
model leverages the information provided by the mechanistic model
itself. This results in a formulation that benefits from both strategies,
without being a conventional instance of either.
Random forest (RF) models are employed as data-driven components
(Breiman, 2001). They make output predictions by combining the out­
comes from a sequence of regression decision trees, called forest; each
tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently
and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest. The output
value for the RF is simply the average value of the outputs for every
decision tree in the forest.
The selection of RFs as data-driven component is motivated by their
ability to capture nonlinear relationships, and because they tend to
perform well in low-data regimes while exhibiting relatively low risk of
overfitting (He and Garcia, 2009). However, it should be noted that the
signal predicted by RFs may appear noisy, since the implementation
does not account for temporal autocorrelation. As a result, the pre­
dictions may lack smoothness, and a filtering step was applied to
dampen these fluctuations (Blackledget, 2006). The moving average ̃yi

RFs demonstrated very good performance in the case studies
